Noncrossing is All You Need: Beyond Identical Delay Functions in Online Matching with Delays on General Metrics

Online optimization with delays has emerged as a powerful paradigm with numerous applications, including matching, caching, server management, network design, and set cover. In most of these problems, competitive algorithms are known for arbitrary monotone delay functions, even when different requests are associated with different delay functions. The notable exception is online matching with delays, where all previously known algorithms achieving constant or polylogarithmic competitive ratios require the delay functions to be identical, either linear or concave, and known in advance.

We study the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delays problem on general metrics. We introduce the broad class of noncrossing delay functions, which strictly generalizes the classic setting of identical concave delay functions while naturally modeling scenarios in which different requests may experience different delay costs. We present the first deterministic O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive algorithm for the single-location online matching problem with noncrossing delay functions in the non-clairvoyant setting as well as a randomized O⁡(log⁡n​log⁡Δ+log2⁡Δ)O(\log n\log\Delta+\log^{2}\Delta)-competitive algorithm of an arbitrary metric space where nn is the number of points of the metric space and Δ\Delta is its aspect ratio. Our result allows each request to have an arbitrary noncrossing delay function, thereby simultaneously removing the assumptions of identical delay functions, concavity, and clairvoyance that were required by all previous constant or polylogarithmic-competitive algorithms.

1 Introduction

Over the last decade, online optimization with delays has emerged as a powerful and widely applicable paradigm. It has been successfully applied to a broad range of problems, including matching, caching, server management, network design, set cover, data structures, and many others (e.g., [13, 23, 7, 4, 11, 22], among many others). In this framework, requests arrive online and may be served at any time after their arrival. Delaying service incurs a request-dependent penalty that increases over time, while postponing decisions may reduce the underlying optimization cost by allowing the algorithm to aggregate requests and serve them in a batch. Consequently, the objective is to decide both which requests to serve and when to serve them so as to minimize the sum of the traditional optimization cost and the accumulated delay penalties. This fundamental trade-off has made the framework both practically relevant and a rich source of algorithmic ideas in the theory of online algorithms.

A remarkable feature shared by nearly all of these problems is that competitive algorithms are known for arbitrary monotone delay functions, even when different requests are associated with different delay functions. The main exception to this phenomenon is the matching problem, first studied by [23], which was also the first problem studied in the online-with-delays framework. All previously known algorithms achieving constant or polylogarithmic competitive ratios require the delay functions to be identical and either linear or concave. In this paper, we break this barrier by presenting, for the first time, competitive algorithms for a broad family of non-identical delay functions.

We note that one possible explanation for why matching is fundamentally different from other online optimization problems with delays is the lack of input monotonicity. For virtually all other problems studied in this framework, adding more requests can only increase (or leave unchanged) the value of the optimal solution. In contrast, for matching, the arrival of additional requests may arbitrarily decrease the optimal cost by creating new matching opportunities. This fundamental non-monotonicity appears to be a major obstacle to extending techniques developed for other online optimization problems with delays to the matching problem.

One motivation for the matching with delays comes from commercial platforms for matching clients or players. Examples include gaming platforms such as chess.com and bridgebase.com, where players arrive online with the intention of participating in a game against another player. Since most games involve exactly two participants, the platform must match arriving players into pairs. While players are generally willing to tolerate some waiting time before being matched, excessive delays reduce user satisfaction. This naturally raises the following algorithmic question: how should the platform match players so as to minimize the overall delay cost?

Beyond gaming platforms, this problem captures a wide range of online matching applications, including roommate assignment, carpooling, and other real-time matching services.

Problem Definition:

In this paper, we study the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delay problem, introduced by [23]. Formally, requests arrive online over time in a metric space (X,d)(X,d). At any point after their arrival, the algorithm may match any pair of unmatched requests or postpone their matching until a later time.

The cost of a matching is determined by how requests are matched into pairs and when they are matched. Each request rr arrives at location ℓ⁡(r)∈X\ell(r)\in X, has an arrival time a⁡(r)a(r), and a delay function fr​(t)f_{r}(t) that starts at 0 at a⁡(r)a(r), and is nondecreasing with time. When rr is matched at time m⁡(r)m(r), it incurs a delay cost of fr​(m​(r))f_{r}(m(r)). If request rr is matched to request r′r^{\prime}, they incur a connection cost of d⁡(ℓ⁡(r),ℓ⁡(r′))d(\ell(r),\ell(r^{\prime})). The total cost of a matching is

∑rfr​(m⁡(r))+∑(r,r′)∈Md⁡(ℓ⁡(r),ℓ⁡(r′)),\sum_{r}f_{r}(m(r))+\sum_{(r,r^{\prime})\in M}d(\ell(r),\ell(r^{\prime})),

where MM is the matching and the objective is to minimize this quantity.

Previous delay setting:

Previous works obtaining constant or polylogarithmic competitive ratios rely simultaneously on the following three assumptions:

  1. 1.

    all requests share the same delay function (shifted by the arrival time)11 1 More specifically, fr​(a⁡(r)+d)=fq​(a⁡(q)+d)f_{r}(a(r)+d)=f_{q}(a(q)+d) for any two requests q,rq,r and d≥0d\geq 0.;

  2. 2.

    the delay function is linear or concave;

  3. 3.

    the delay function is known upon the request’s arrival (i.e., the algorithm is clairvoyant).

The MPMD problem was introduced by [23], who studied the case of linear delay functions. Later, the authors in [31] considered convex delay functions and posed the question of whether comparable competitive guarantees could be obtained for concave delay functions. This question was subsequently answered by [9], who developed competitive algorithms for the concave setting.

Our delay setting:

In contrast, we study a substantially more general setting in which

  1. 1.

    each request may have a different delay function;

  2. 2.

    delay functions are arbitrary noncrossing functions (defined formally in Section 2);

  3. 3.

    the algorithm is non-clairvoyant, namely, for every request that has already arrived, its delay function is revealed only up to the current time, and its future behavior is unknown.

Informally, noncrossing delay functions form a sequence of functions in which, at every point in time, an earlier request always has a delay value at least as large as that of any later request, while its derivative is never larger. Observe that noncrossing delay functions generalize the classic setting of identical concave delay functions studied by [9]. Noncrossing delay functions naturally arise in practice. Earlier clients are typically more frustrated than later arrivals, and their frustration may evolve in an arbitrary manner depending on external circumstances, rather than following a pre-defined concave shape. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to assume that, at any point in time, an earlier client is never less frustrated than a later one, while the rate at which this frustration increases is never higher than that of a later client.

Our Contributions:

In this paper, we consider both the single location case and an arbitrary metric space. We present the first deterministic O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive algorithm for the single-location online matching problem with noncrossing delay functions in the nonclairvoyant setting. For general metrics with nn points and aspect ratio Δ\Delta, we obtain a randomized O⁡(log⁡n​log⁡Δ+log2⁡Δ)O(\log n\log\Delta+\log^{2}\Delta)-competitive algorithm. Our algorithms allow arbitrary request-specific delay functions subject only to the noncrossing condition, thereby simultaneously removing the assumptions of identical delay functions, concavity, and clairvoyance imposed by previous constant or polylogarithmic-competitive algorithms.

Theorem 1.1.

For any metric space with nn points and aspect ratio Δ\Delta, there is a randomized nonclairvoyant O⁡(log⁡n​log⁡Δ+log2⁡Δ)O(\log n\log\Delta+\log^{2}\Delta)-competitive algorithm for the online matching problem with noncrossing delay functions. For the special case of a single location, there is a deterministic nonclairvoyant O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive algorithm.

We also show that it is impossible for any deterministic clairvoyant algorithm to achieve a bounded competitive ratio without the assumption that an earlier request always has a delay cost at least as large as that of any later request, even for the single point case. See in .

Geometric Interpretation for single location:

Our problem for the very special case of single location admits the following equivalent geometric interpretation. Points are born over time at the origin and continuously move to the right along the xx-axis, where the xx-coordinate of a point represents its accumulated delay. The relative order of the points is preserved over time (by the noncrossing property), and the distance between any two consecutive points—and hence between any pair of points—never increases. At any time, the algorithm may freeze any pair of points, remove them from the system, and incur a cost equal to the sum of their current positions, corresponding to matching the two associated requests. Every point must eventually be frozen. The objective is to minimize the total freezing cost, which is exactly the total delay incurred before all requests are matched.

Despite this simple and intuitive formulation, designing a constant-competitive online algorithm, and proving its competitiveness, turns out to be remarkably challenging. An obvious first approach is to match the requests greedily (i.e., delay only if there is no other request). While this yields an optimal matching when delay functions are identical and linear (or convex), unfortunately, as observed by [9], the simple greedy matching algorithm has unbounded competitive ratio even for identical concave delay functions. To see this, consider an instance in which 2​m2m requests arrive at times {0}∪{i,i+ε}i=1m−1∪{m}\{0\}\cup\{i,i+\varepsilon\}_{i=1}^{m-1}\cup\{m\} and the delay function of each request rr is given by fr​(t)=min⁡{t−a⁡(r),1}f_{r}(t)=\min\{t-a(r),1\}. The greedy algorithm incurs a total cost of 1+(1−ε)​(m−1)1+(1-\varepsilon)(m-1). In contrast, the optimal solution matches the first request with the last and matches all remaining requests greedily, thereby yielding a total cost of 1+(m−1)​ε1+(m-1)\varepsilon. By choosing ε\varepsilon sufficiently small, the competitive ratio of the greedy algorithm becomes at least mm, and is therefore unbounded. This example illustrates that achieving a bounded competitive ratio requires sacrificing short-term cost in order to obtain greater future savings.

Arbitrary metric space versus single location.

As explained above, even the single-location case, a highly restricted special case of a general metric space—requires a nontrivial algorithm. Surprisingly, our first technique is to “reduce” the general case to single-location problems. We use a hierarchically separated tree (HST) and run a single-location algorithm at each vertex, processing requests promoted from its children according to a carefully designed rule.

This is not a reduction in the usual sense, as it requires a stronger guarantee than competitiveness for the single-location problem. Specifically, at each vertex, we compare the cost of the online algorithm on the requests that reach that vertex, the “virtual instance” (which filters out some of the requests), with the optimal cost for all requests originating in its subtree, the “consolidated instance”. Thus, the online algorithm and the offline optimum operate on different instances. Although this “pseudo-reduction” requires a more powerful single-location result, it significantly simplifies the analysis of the general metric case. The main challenge then lies in designing and analyzing a single-location algorithm that admits this stronger comparison between the virtual instance and consolidated instances, though even the standard single-location problem is not substantially simpler. This “pseudo-reduction” incurs a multiplicative loss proportional to the height of the HST, which is O⁡(log⁡Δ)O(\log\Delta), together with an additional O⁡(log⁡Δ)O(\log\Delta) loss in the delay-cost term alone. Embedding the original metric space into HSTs introduces an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) distortion in the connection-cost term. Since the latter two losses affect separate cost components, they combine additively. Accounting for the initial height-dependent loss, the resulting competitive ratio is O⁡(log⁡Δ⁡(log⁡n+log⁡Δ))=O⁡(log⁡n​log​Δ+log2⁡Δ)O(\log\Delta(\log n+\log\Delta))=O(\log n\log\Delta+\log^{2}\Delta).

1.1 Our Techniques

As we already discussed the pseudo-reduction from an arbitrary metric space to virtual single location instances, most of this subsection deals with an actual single location instance which includes most of the new ideas and techniques. At the end we mention the additional difference that we encounter while switching from to comparing the virtual instance (which filters out some of the requests) to the consolidate instance for generalizing our algorithm from a single location to an arbitrary metric space.

Our work builds on the technique of matching based on counters that increase over time, which is central to previous works on online matching with delays, and develops new insight on this technique. The main challenge is in designing the matching condition so that the following desiderata are satisfied: (1) the total counter value captures the cost of the algorithm and (2) is also not much larger than the cost of the optimal solution. Intuitively, an equivalent view is that the algorithm matches when the cost of the match can be charged to some set of counters which can then be charged to the optimal solution.

As our problem, even for single location, generalizes the single-location problem of [9], it is useful to contrast our approach with theirs. Our algorithm differs significantly from theirs, which relies heavily on the fact that all delay functions are identical. In particular, that algorithm maintains counters that are shared among all requests. In contrast, in our setting it is natural to associate a separate counter with each request. Whenever a request’s counter increases, it does so at the same rate as its delay function.

It is not difficult to see that it suffices to consider algorithms that match only the latest two pending requests (only for the single location case), since later requests always have delay derivatives at least as large as those of earlier requests. To ensure that the matching condition is eventually satisfied for the last two pending requests, our algorithm increases only the counter of the latest pending request.

Unfortunately, as demonstrated by our first two attempts, the counter values alone do not provide sufficient information to determine when a match should be performed. This is in sharp contrast to previous algorithms, where the counters alone were sufficient. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a carefully designed potential function based on a partition of the requests, as described later.

First attempt.

Motivated by the counterexample to the greedy algorithm, a natural first attempt is to wait until the latest request’s counter reaches half of the second latest request to make a match. It also has the benefit that all pending requests’ counter values form a geometric sequence at every moment, and thus the total delay seems to be bounded by the biggest term, i.e. the counter value of the earliest request. Unfortunately, it does not work under uniform linear delays. Intuitively, it fails because it matches requests too slowly while the previous requests have already accumulated huge cost. In particular, its cost can be much larger than the total counter value. See for a specific counterexample.

Second attempt.

The first attempt can be seen in the following way: the second latest request rr’s counter value is saturated from below when the latest request’s counter reaches half of its value. It fails because of the “memorylessness” that saturates too slowly. A natural way around this is to consider not only the latest request at a given moment, but also all previous requests that used to be the next pending request after rr (we will use “children” of rr to denote them in Section 4.1) and all their counters contribute to the saturation of rr’s counter.

Therefore, our second attempt is to match when the sum of counter values of all children of rr reaches half of the second latest request rr’s counter value. Under this algorithm, the counter value of each request is within a constant factor of its actual incurred delay, so the issue with the counterexample of the first attempt is addressed. Unfortunately, this algorithm also fails because it might match “too fast” instead, and the total counter value can be much larger than the cost of the optimal solution. We present the counterexample in . In this example, the requests’ delays have similar patterns to concave delays: initially increasing fast but stopping at some value; while we note that they are not uniform concave delays and the delay function of a given request may not be concave either.

In summary, both attempts fail to match requests at an appropriate speed under some cases, including linear delays that grow fast and other delays that grow slowly. This also illustrates that our noncrossing delay model comprises a broad range of ways that delays can evolve over time. The first attempt shows that the algorithm cannot be memoryless, and the second attempt shows that such memory cannot be the simple sum of all children’s counters of the second latest request.

Partition-based potential.

At a high level, our algorithm assigns a potential to each pending request based on the counter values of its current children. The potential is designed so that, at any point in time, only one child can increase the potential of its parent. The algorithm matches a pair of requests once the potential of the earlier request reaches half of its counter value. This perspective also unifies the two previously discussed failed attempts: they correspond to defining the potential as either the counter of a single child or the sum of the counters of all current children. Roughly speaking, the potential measures the amount of delay incurred by the optimal solution that can be safely charged by our algorithm. The potential function and the matching rule are carefully designed so that a request is matched precisely when its accumulated counter value can be fully charged to the optimal solution without causing any overcharging.

The key ingredient in our charging argument is a decomposition of the requests that arrive after a given request according to the intervals used by the optimal solution. We consider the maximal intervals of the optimal solution that overlap the lifetime of the request without completely covering it. These intervals partition the requests that arrive while the request is pending. Unfortunately, since the optimal solution is unknown, the corresponding partition is also unknown. Instead of relying on this partition directly, we define the potential function to represent the value of the minimum-value partition.

Now consider one such interval that contains several consecutive children of the request but not the request itself. Since the interval begins before the first of these children arrives and remains active until after all but the last have been matched, the noncrossing property implies that the delay accumulated by the request during this period is no larger than the delay incurred by that interval in the optimal solution. This observation enables us to charge the delay accumulated over each such period to the corresponding interval of the optimal solution without overcharging.

Handling virtual instances for HSTs.

When extending our single-location algorithm to HSTs, we construct a virtual instance at each vertex by filtering out certain requests arriving in its subtree. Counter updates at an internal vertex must also account for the parity of the number of pending requests in its subtree, a quantity also used in earlier counter-based algorithms on trees ([3, 9]). Accordingly, the virtual algorithm at each vertex has an odd state and an even state, determined by this parity, which specifies which counter to increase.

A key difference from the single-location algorithm discussed earlier is that we do not necessarily increase the counter of the latest request. As a result, the property that the algorithm always matches the latest two requests no longer holds, and the laminarity of the solution may fail. To address this issue, we sometimes terminate a request’s current interval and counter and create new ones corresponding to the same request. This allows us to partition the pending time of each request into multiple intervals, with the resulting collection of intervals being laminar. In this way, we can adapt the proof techniques developed for the single-location case to those laminar intervals and their associated counters.

1.2 Related Work

The MPMD problem with linear delay functions was introduced by [23], who presented a randomized algorithm with competitive ratio O⁡(log2⁡n+log⁡Δ)O(\log^{2}n+\log\Delta), where Δ\Delta denotes the aspect ratio of the underlying metric. Later, [3] improved this bound to O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), thereby eliminating the dependence on Δ\Delta. They also proved an Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\sqrt{\log n}) lower bound on the competitive ratio of any randomized algorithm. This lower bound was subsequently strengthened by the authors in [2] to Ω⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Omega(\log n/\log\log n), nearly closing the gap. The upper bound of O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) was later generalized for identical concave delay functions by [9].

The authors in [31] later studied MPMD with convex delay functions on nn-point uniform metrics. They first established an Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) lower bound on the competitive ratio of any deterministic algorithm. Their lower-bound construction uses delay functions of the form f⁡(t)=tαf(t)=t^{\alpha}, for α>1\alpha>1. They also presented a deterministic O⁡(n)O(n)-competitive algorithm under the same class of delay functions. [28] complemented this study by presenting a deterministic O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive algorithm for polynomial delays such that f′​(0)>0f^{\prime}(0)>0.

The only non-clairvoyant delay models that have been studied in prior works are set and size-based delays proposed by Deryckere and Umboh [20]. They showed a deterministic lower bound of Ω⁡(Δ)\Omega(\Delta) for set delays and gave a randomized upper bound of O⁡(m4)O(m^{4}) for size-based delays, where mm is the number of requests. The results on size-based delays were subsequently improved by [28] and they showed that the randomized competitive ratio is Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) and O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) for every metric, refuting the possibility of a polylogarithmic competitive ratio.

A related line of work considers Minimum-Cost Bipartite Perfect Matching with Delays (MBPMD), the bipartite variant of MPMD with linear delay functions, in which requests can only be matched to requests of the opposite polarity. The authors in [2] established an Ω⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Omega(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n}) lower bound on the competitive ratio of any randomized algorithm. They also presented two O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-competitive randomized algorithms: the first extends the algorithm of [23] to the bipartite setting, while the second extends the algorithm of [3].

The deterministic variants of MPMD and MBPMD with linear delay functions have also attracted considerable attention. For deterministic algorithms and further developments, see [15, 14, 6, 22, 1, 24].

Although this paper focuses on online matching with delays, the notion of delays has been extensively studied in many other online optimization problems. Such models have numerous applications spanning operations management, operating systems, supply chain management, and other domains. Examples include the online service with delays problem [7, 16, 10], the multi-level aggregation problem [13, 17, 10], and many others. For a broader overview of online optimization problems with delays, we refer the reader to [18, 29, 25, 5, 4, 11, 34, 19, 36].

Finally, we note that in other optimization problems with delays, there has been much recent interest in studying the power of clairvoyance [4, 30, 35, 37, 26, 21] and novel delay models [32, 8, 33, 12].

Paper Organization:

We start in Section 2 by formally defining the problem and introducing some useful notations and basic properties, including laminar solutions and randomized embedding of general metrics into σ\sigma-HSTs. We introduce the pseudo-reduction to single-location instances in Section 3, and present our algorithm on a 22-HST of height HH by describing the algorithms that run on each of its vertices in Section 4. We prove that our global algorithm is (O⁡(H),O⁡(H2))(O(H),O(H^{2}))-competitive on the 22-HST in Section 5, thus completing the proof of Theorem 1.1. We conclude with some remarks and open problems in Section 6.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Problem Definition and Notation

In the online matching with delays problem, a set ℛ\mathcal{R} of requests arrive over time (we assume WLOG that no two requests arrive at the same time) in a given metric space (X,d)(X,d), and each request incurs delay cost until it is matched with another request. More precisely, each request rr has a location ℓ⁡(r)∈X\ell(r)\in X, and a continuous delay function fr​(t)f_{r}(t) that is initially 0 at the arrival time of rr, which we denote by a⁡(r)a(r), and is nondecreasing with time. In addition, we assume that the algorithm is nonclairvoyant: at every moment tt, the algorithm receives fr′​(t)f^{\prime}_{r}(t), the instantaneous delay increase rate of rr, for every request a⁡(r)≤ta(r)\leq t that has arrived.

A solution to the problem consists of a pair (M,m)(M,m) where MM is a matching, and m⁡(r)m(r) is the time when request rr is matched, for each request rr. When requests r,r′r,r^{\prime} are matched, we denote the match as (r,r′)(r,r^{\prime}) writing the requests in order of arrival, i.e., rr arrives earlier. When request rr is matched at time m⁡(r)m(r), the total delay incurred is fr​(m​(r))f_{r}(m(r)). The goal is to match the requests so as to minimize the total delay of requests (delay cost) plus the distance between locations of every matched pair (connection cost), i.e., ∑r∈ℛfr​(m⁡(r))+∑(r,r′)∈Md⁡(ℓ⁡(r),ℓ⁡(r′))\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}f_{r}(m(r))+\sum_{(r,r^{\prime})\in M}d(\ell(r),\ell(r^{\prime})).

For I⊆ℝ+I\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{+}, we write fr​(I)=∫t∈Ifr′​(t)​𝑑tf_{r}(I)=\int_{t\in I}f^{\prime}_{r}(t)dt and fr​(m⁡(r))=∫t∈[a⁡(r),m⁡(r))fr′​(t)​𝑑tf_{r}(m(r))=\int_{t\in[a(r),m(r))}f^{\prime}_{r}(t)dt. Throughout the paper, for a set of requests SS, we write “ii-th latest request of SS” to refer to the request in SS with the ii-th latest arrival time. For any two requests r1,r2r_{1},r_{2}, we write r1⪯r2r_{1}\preceq r_{2} if a⁡(r1)≤a⁡(r2)a(r_{1})\leq a(r_{2}), and r1≺r2r_{1}\prec r_{2} if a⁡(r1)<a⁡(r2)a(r_{1})<a(r_{2}).

Definition 2.1 (Noncrossing delays).

An instance ℛ\mathcal{R} has noncrossing delays if for every r1≺r2r_{1}\prec r_{2}, it holds that fr1′​(t)≤fr2′​(t)f_{r_{1}}^{\prime}(t)\leq f^{\prime}_{r_{2}}(t) and fr1​(t)≥fr2​(t)f_{r_{1}}(t)\geq f_{r_{2}}(t) at every time t≥a⁡(r2)t\geq a(r_{2}).

Noncrossing delays means that the delay of every request increases at least as fast as the delay of an earlier-arriving request, but its total delay is no larger than the total delay of the earlier-arriving request. Equivalently, for any two requests, the difference in their total delays is always nonincreasing and nonnegative.

2.2 Laminar Solutions

In this part, we introduce the concept of laminarity, which is an important property that holds for every optimal solution on a single location instance (where the connection cost is always zero). Furthermore, the laminar property of a family of intervals will be used in defining our algorithm on metrics as well.

Definition 2.2 (Request intervals and laminarity).

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be a single-point instance where requests’ delays are non-crossing and (M,m)(M,m) be a solution of ℐ\mathcal{I}. For each request rr, define its interval to be Ir=[a⁡(r),m⁡(r))I_{r}=[a(r),m(r)). The solution is a laminar solution if the set of intervals IrI_{r} is laminar.

The following is immediate from the definition.

Proposition 2.3.

A solution (M,m)(M,m) is laminar if and only if for every request rr and every request r′r^{\prime} with arrival time a⁡(r′)∈(a⁡(r),m⁡(r))a(r^{\prime})\in(a(r),m(r)), m⁡(r′)≤m⁡(r)m(r^{\prime})\leq m(r).

From Proposition 2.3, it is easy to see that an online algorithm that only matches the latest two pending requests is laminar. Moreover, since there is an optimal solution that only matches the latest two pending requests on a single-location instance (because their delays increase at the fastest rate), and the optimal solution always matches a pair of requests as soon as they have both arrived to avoid additional delay, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 2.4.

For online matching with noncrossing delays on a single location, there is an optimal solution (M∗,m∗)(M^{*},m^{*}) that is laminar, and every match (r,r′)∈M∗(r,r^{\prime})\in M^{*} is matched on arrival of the later request r′r^{\prime}.

Although the laminarity of the optimal solution does not hold on metric spaces beyond the single location, we will use Lemma 2.4 in the charging scheme for our algorithm analysis.

2.3 Reduction to 22-HSTs

We solve the online matching with noncrossing delay on general metrics by reducing it to 22-HSTs. This is the key technique that has been used for all previous results of the online matching with delay problem on general metrics, e.g. [23, 3, 9]. We introduce the definition of a (β,γ)(\beta,\gamma)-competitive algorithm to separate delay and connection costs.

Definition 2.5.

For an arbitrary instance of online matching with noncrossing delays, let 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} be a randomized online algorithm and its cost and 𝖲𝖮𝖫\mathsf{SOL} be an arbitrary solution. Furthermore, 𝖲𝖮𝖫d\mathsf{SOL}_{d} and 𝖲𝖮𝖫t\mathsf{SOL}_{t} denote the connection and delay costs incurred by 𝖲𝖮𝖫\mathsf{SOL}, respectively. We say that 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} is (β,γ)(\beta,\gamma)-competitive if 𝔼⁡[𝖠𝖫𝖦]≤β⋅𝖲𝖮𝖫d+γ⋅𝖲𝖮𝖫t\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{ALG}]\leq\beta\cdot\mathsf{SOL}_{d}+\gamma\cdot\mathsf{SOL}_{t}.

The reason that we focus on solving the problem on σ\sigma-HSTs is because we can randomly embed general metrics into them. We first formally define the notion of Hierarchically Separated Trees (HSTs) and embedding a metric into another.

Definition 2.6 (σ\sigma-HST).

A σ\sigma-hierarchically well-separated tree (σ\sigma-HST) is a rooted tree such that: all edges at a particular level have the same weight and all leaves are at the same level (combinatorial depth), and edge lengths on every root-to-leaf path decrease by a factor of σ\sigma at each step.

Note that in our definition, we require that every leaf has the same combinatorial depth. This key requirement is the reason that we cannot use weighted HSTs to reduce the height as per the techniques that have been used for linear and concave delays [3, 9].

Definition 2.7 (Metric embeddings).

Let ℳ=(X,d)\mathcal{M}=(X,d) be a finite metric space, and let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be a probability distribution over metrics on a finite set X′X^{\prime}. We say that ℳ\mathcal{M} embeds into 𝒟\mathcal{D} if X⊆X′X\subseteq X^{\prime}, and for every x,y∈Xx,y\in X and every metric space ℳ′=(X′,d′)\mathcal{M}^{\prime}=(X^{\prime},d^{\prime}) in the support of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we have d⁡(x,y)≤d′​(x,y)d(x,y)\leq d^{\prime}(x,y). The distortion of this embedding is defined to be

maxx≠y∈X⁡𝔼ℳ′=(X′,d′)∼𝒟​[d′​(x,y)]d⁡(x,y).\max_{x\neq y\in X}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}=(X^{\prime},d^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}}[d^{\prime}(x,y)]}{d(x,y)}.

We use the following result from [27] to embed any general nn-point metric with aspect ratio Δ\Delta into a distribution over 22-HSTs.

Lemma 2.8.

Any nn-point metric can be embedded, with distortion O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), into a distribution supported on metrics induced by 22-HSTs with height O⁡(log⁡Δ)O(\log\Delta).

The next lemma introduced in [23] shows how to convert a matching’s cost from a metric in the support of the embedding to that on the original metric.

Lemma 2.9.

Suppose that a metric ℳ\mathcal{M} can be embedded into a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} with distortion μ\mu. Additionally suppose that for every metric space in the support of 𝒟\mathcal{D} exists an algorithm that is (β,γ)(\beta,\gamma)-competitive for the MPMD problem. Then, there exists a (μ​β,γ)(\mu\beta,\gamma)-competitive algorithm for the MPMD problem on the metric ℳ\mathcal{M}.

In remaining parts of the paper, we describe the algorithm on a 22-HST whose height is HH (including the root level), denoted by 𝒯=(V,E)\mathcal{T}=(V,E). For every vertex u∈Vu\in V, let LuL_{u} be the distance between uu and its leaf descendant, TuT_{u} be the subtree rooted at uu, and p⁡(u)p(u) be its parent. From the definition of 22-HSTs and properties of geometric sequences, we have Lp⁡(u)≥2​LuL_{p(u)}\geq 2L_{u} as long as uu is not the root of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. If uu is the root, then define Lp⁡(u)=∞L_{p(u)}=\infty. Moreover, we use ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u} to express the set of all requests that arrive at leaves of TuT_{u}. For an interval I⊆ℝ+I\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{+}, we define Ru​(I)={r∈ℛu∣a⁡(r)∈I}R_{u}(I)=\{r\in\mathcal{R}_{u}\mid a(r)\in I\}, i.e., the set of requests that arrive at leaves of TuT_{u} during II.

3 A Pseudo-Reduction to Single-Location Instances

In Section 3.1, we reduce the description of our algorithm 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} on 𝒯\mathcal{T} to its subroutines 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} for each vertex uu of the HST, including the requests that arrive in each instance ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, and how we translate 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} to 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} while losing a constant factor only (Lemma 3.1). In Section 3.2, we introduce the consolidated instance induced within each TuT_{u} (Definition 3.3) and prove their relations with any global solution 𝖲𝖮𝖫\mathsf{SOL} (Lemma 3.4), which will be used in proving the competitive ratio of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}. We abuse the notations by using 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} and 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} to refer to both the solution and its cost, the same for 𝖲𝖮𝖫\mathsf{SOL} and 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} (defined in Section 3.2).

3.1 Transform Virtual Algorithms 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s to 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}

Algorithm overview.

Our algorithm 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} creates several single-location instances ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} for each vertex uu of the HST; these are called virtual instances. The requests in the virtual instances are called virtual copies of actual requests. The arrivals of virtual copies in virtual instances are based on a global mechanism where 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} promotes every request to different levels of its ancestors based on its total incurred delay. We then run a single-location algorithm on each of these instances independently. When two virtual copies of requests are matched, the global algorithm decides whether or not to match the corresponding actual requests. We will prove that the total cost of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} is within a constant factor of that of all 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s:

Lemma 3.1 (Reduction to Single-Location).

𝖠𝖫𝖦≤4​∑u∈V𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}\leq 4\sum_{u\in V}\mathsf{ALG}_{u}.

Virtual instances.

At every moment tt, we say that a pending request rr’s position is uu if uu is the ancestor of its leaf location ℓ⁡(r)\ell(r) (or ℓ⁡(r)\ell(r) itself) such that Lu≤fr​(t)<Lp⁡(u)L_{u}\leq f_{r}(t)<L_{p(u)}. Each request’s position is uniquely defined at every moment when it is unmatched by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} (note that the position of rr is different from its location ℓ⁡(r)\ell(r), where the latter is its arrival location in the metric).

We now describe the single-location virtual instance ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} for each u∈Vu\in V. For each request rr that arrives at ℓ⁡(r)\ell(r) and vertex uu that is an ancestor of ℓ⁡(r)\ell(r), a virtual copy of it arrives in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} the moment tt when fr​(t)=Luf_{r}(t)=L_{u}. Or equivalently, its arrival time in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} is the earliest moment when rr’s position is uu (rr is promoted to uu). Since each rr creates at most one such virtual copy in any ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, we still use rr to denote this virtual copy without ambiguity.

After the arrival of virtual rr in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, its delay increase in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} is the delay increase of rr while its position is uu. We emphasize that, later on, when the position of the virtual rr is an ancestor of uu, the virtual copy of rr remains in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} and its delay in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} stops increasing after fr​(t)f_{r}(t) reaches Lp⁡(u)L_{p(u)}. In summary, the delay function fu,r​(t)f_{u,r}(t) of a request rr that arrives in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} at time fr−1​(Lu)f_{r}^{-1}(L_{u}) (without loss of generality, assume that fr′​(t)>0f_{r}^{\prime}(t)>0 for every rr and t≥a⁡(r)t\geq a(r), then fr​(t)f_{r}(t) is a bijection) can be expressed as:

fu,r​(t)={fr​(t)−Luwhen Lu≤fr​(t)<Lp⁡(u);Lp⁡(u)−Luwhen fr​(t)≥Lp⁡(u).f_{u,r}(t)=\begin{cases}f_{r}(t)-L_{u}&\text{when $L_{u}\leq f_{r}(t)<L_{p(u)}$;}\\ L_{p(u)}-L_{u}&\text{when $f_{r}(t)\geq L_{p(u)}$.}\end{cases}

In other words, ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} receives part of request rr’s delay increase while its total value is between LuL_{u} and Lp⁡(u)L_{p(u)}. It is easy to see that the delays fu,r​(t)f_{u,r}(t) for virtual copies of rr in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} satisfy the non-crossing properties as well, and this is why we treat each ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} as a virtual instance. We note that those virtual instances of different vertices are not independent of each other, because the set of requests that are promoted to uu depends on the output of other instances whose vertices are in the subtree TuT_{u}: ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} only receives requests that have not been matched by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} when their positions are descendants of uu, and we can regard 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}’s matches of requests positioned at descendants of uu as a filter removing some requests from ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}.

We observe that when rr is positioned at uu, its delay increase rate in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} is fu,r′​(t)=fr′​(t)f^{\prime}_{u,r}(t)=f^{\prime}_{r}(t), otherwise fu,r′​(t)=0f^{\prime}_{u,r}(t)=0 if rr has been promoted to a higher level. The next observation is immediate from the mechanism of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}’s promotion of requests to different levels based on their total delays and the symmetric structure of a HST.

Observation 3.2.

For every u∈Vu\in V, the arrival order of requests in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} is the same order as in the actual instance. Moreover, if r1r_{1}’s position is u1u_{1} and r2r_{2}’s position is u2u_{2} such that u2u_{2} is a descendant of u1u_{1}, then r1≺r2r_{1}\prec r_{2}.

We will use it in our charging method for analysis.

Virtual to actual matches.

Now we describe how to transform the virtual matches produced by 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s to the actual solution output by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}. For every vertex uu, if 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} matches two requests r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}, then there are two cases according to whether the position of each of r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} is uu at the moment. If r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} both are still positioned at uu, then 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} matches r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} the moment when they are matched by 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}. If at least one of r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} has been promoted to a higher level, then 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} “ignores” the action of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} matching them and both of them will be promoted to p⁡(u)p(u) when the total delay reaches Lp⁡(u)L_{p(u)}, and how each of r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} is eventually matched by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} will depend on other sub-routines at ancestors of uu. As a result, the actual matches produced by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} can be significantly different from those made by its sub-routines 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s.

The proof of Lemma 3.1 can be found in the Appendix. As a result, with 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}’s global mechanism of promoting requests to different levels of their ancestors, it suffices to describe the sub-algorithm 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} for each vertex u∈Vu\in V in Section 4.

3.2 Consolidated Instances

For every u∈Vu\in V, we define a consolidated single-location instance comprising all requests whose locations are within TuT_{u}, the subtree rooted at uu.

Definition 3.3 (Consolidated instance induced within TuT_{u}).

The input request set is the same as ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u}, all requests whose locations are leaves of TuT_{u}. For every request r∈ℛur\in\mathcal{R}_{u}, its arrival time in the consolidated instance is also a⁡(r)a(r) as in the original instance on 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The total delay incurred by rr until tt if unmatched is equal to f^r​(t)=min⁡{fr​(t),Lp⁡(u)}\hat{f}_{r}(t)=\min\{f_{r}(t),L_{p(u)}\}, i.e. it increases at the same rate as fr​(t)f_{r}(t) until its value is capped by Lp⁡(u)L_{p(u)}.

It is easy to see that such delays are non-crossing. However, different from the conventional online matching with delays, here for each uu that is not the root of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the number of requests in the instance is not necessarily even, i.e. there might be requests unmatched at the end. Since the delay function of each request is capped by a constant Lp⁡(u)L_{p(u)}, this is the cost of leaving one request unmatched, and so the objective is well-defined. We also note this consolidated instance is different from the virtual instance ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} that is described in Section 3.1: here every request that arrives within TuT_{u} is counted from its arrival time, rather than the moment when it is promoted to uu, and the consolidated instance includes those not promoted to uu by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} as well. This is why we call it a “pseudo-reduction”, because we compare the cost of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} against a different instance. For every request r∈ℛur\in\mathcal{R}_{u}, it holds that f^r​(t)≥fu,r​(t)\hat{f}_{r}(t)\geq f_{u,r}(t) and f^r′​(t)=fu,r′​(t)\hat{f}^{\prime}_{r}(t)=f^{\prime}_{u,r}(t) for all t≥fr−1​(Lu)t\geq f_{r}^{-1}(L_{u}).

We use 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} to denote the optimal solution as well as its cost of the consolidated instance induced within TuT_{u}. Without loss of generality, we assume that 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} is laminar (Lemma 2.4), and it matches all requests into pairs if |ℛu||\mathcal{R}_{u}| is even and leaves exactly one request unmatched if |ℛu||\mathcal{R}_{u}| is odd.

Given a solution 𝖲𝖮𝖫\mathsf{SOL} of the online matching with noncrossing delay instance on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, let 𝖲𝖮𝖫d\mathsf{SOL}_{d} be its connection cost and 𝖲𝖮𝖫t\mathsf{SOL}_{t} be its delay cost. Moreover, for every vertex uu, we use 𝖲𝖮𝖫u,d\mathsf{SOL}_{u,d} to denote its cost of using the edge connecting uu and p⁡(u)p(u) to make a match (zero if uu is the root) and 𝖲𝖮𝖫u,t\mathsf{SOL}_{u,t} to denote part of its delay cost incurred by requests whose locations are within TuT_{u}. It holds that 𝖲𝖮𝖫d=∑u∈V𝖲𝖮𝖫u,d\mathsf{SOL}_{d}=\sum_{u\in V}\mathsf{SOL}_{u,d} and H⋅𝖲𝖮𝖫t=∑u∈V𝖲𝖮𝖫u,tH\cdot\mathsf{SOL}_{t}=\sum_{u\in V}\mathsf{SOL}_{u,t}, where the latter is because the delay incurred by each request is counted for HH times along the path from its leaf location to the root.

We now establish the relation between 𝖲𝖮𝖫\mathsf{SOL} and 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}’s, whose proof we defer to the Appendix.

Lemma 3.4 (Consolidated to Global).

For any solution 𝖲𝖮𝖫\mathsf{SOL}, ∑u∈V𝖮𝖯𝖳^u≤2​𝖲𝖮𝖫d+H⋅𝖲𝖮𝖫t\sum_{u\in V}\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}\leq 2\mathsf{SOL}_{d}+H\cdot\mathsf{SOL}_{t}.

With Lemmas 3.1 and 3.4, to prove the competitive ratio of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}, it suffices to compare the total cost of all 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s against that of all 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}’s. At the end of Section 5, we will show that ∑u∈V𝖠𝖫𝖦u≤O⁡(1)​∑u∈V𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{u\in V}\mathsf{ALG}_{u}\leq O(1)\sum_{u\in V}\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} (Lemma 5.31).

In the remainder of the algorithm description and analysis, we may consider each vertex uu separately by fixing u∈Vu\in V and only considering request arrivals within TuT_{u} without explicitly specifying it every single time.

4 Single-Location Algorithms

In this section, we define 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} for every uu, which completes the description of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} combined with the way to translate 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s to 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} that has been defined in Section 3.1. In Section 4.1, we use laminarity defined in Section 2.2 to define a forest structure of laminar intervals, which is key to applying tree terminologies including parents and children to the potential function and algorithm in Section 4.2.

4.1 Forest Structure of Laminar Intervals

In this subsection, we fix a vertex uu of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and define a forest structure ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) that evolves over time, where each node represents a time interval (we reserve “vertices” to mean vertices of 𝒯\mathcal{T} and “nodes” to mean those of the forest ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t)). Moreover, the intervals in the forest form a laminar family, and the interval of each node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is a subset of the pending time of a request that arrives in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, which we use r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) to denote. We also call r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) the request of node 𝔫\mathfrak{n}. On the other hand, we note that the solution of the single-point instance ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} itself is not necessarily laminar as those intervals in the forest are not the same as the request pending intervals.

We use 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u} to denote the set of all nodes that are added to ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) at some time tt. Once a node is added to ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t), it will never be deleted, while it can be terminated. We use au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) to denote the moment when node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is added to ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) (we also call it the arrival time of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}), and mu​(𝔫)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) to denote the moment when 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is terminated, for which the conditions we will specify later. For each node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} of ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t), we define the notion of online node intervals at moment tt.

Definition 4.1 (Online intervals).

Given an online algorithm on ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, the interval I𝔫​(t)I_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) at time tt of node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is defined as follows:

I𝔫​(t)={[au​(𝔫),mu​(𝔫))if 𝔫 has already been terminated[au​(𝔫),t)otherwiseI_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)=\begin{cases}[a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}),m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))&\text{if $\mathfrak{n}$ has already been terminated}\\ [a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}),t)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

Same as the terminology that we use for requests, for a set of nodes SS in 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u}, we write “ii-th latest node of SS” to refer to the node in SS with the ii-th latest arrival time. For any two nodes 𝔫1,𝔫2∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}_{1},\mathfrak{n}_{2}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, we write 𝔫1⪯u𝔫2\mathfrak{n}_{1}\preceq_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{2} if au​(𝔫1)≤au​(𝔫2)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{1})\leq a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{2}), and 𝔫1≺u𝔫2\mathfrak{n}_{1}\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{2} if au​(𝔫1)<au​(𝔫2)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{1})<a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{2}).

Without specifying the exact rules of matching requests of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}, for this part we only need the following property to make the laminar forest structure well-defined:

Property 4.2.

At every moment, among all currently live nodes 𝔫1≺u…≺u𝔫k\mathfrak{n}_{1}\prec_{u}\ldots\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{k} and their requests r⁡(𝔫1),…,r⁡(𝔫k)r(\mathfrak{n}_{1}),\ldots,r(\mathfrak{n}_{k}), the online algorithm only matches either r⁡(𝔫k−1)r(\mathfrak{n}_{k-1}) and r⁡(𝔫k)r(\mathfrak{n}_{k}), or r⁡(𝔫k−2)r(\mathfrak{n}_{k-2}) and r⁡(𝔫k−1)r(\mathfrak{n}_{k-1}).

We will see later in Section 4.2 that 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} indeed satisfies this property.

Update rules of ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t).

Now we define the rules of updating ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t), given any online algorithm of ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} that satisfies Property 4.2. There are two events that change the structure of ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t): when a new request arrives in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, and when two requests are matched by the online algorithm.

When a request qq arrives in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, if there is no live node, then we create a new node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} that is the root of a new tree in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t), and let r⁡(𝔫)=qr(\mathfrak{n})=q. If 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is the latest live node right before qq arrives in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, then we create a new node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} as a child of 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} and let r⁡(𝔫)=qr(\mathfrak{n})=q.

When two requests are matched, if they are the requests of the latest two live nodes in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) at the moment, then we terminate those two nodes; if they are the requests of the third and second latest live nodes, then we terminate those two nodes together with the latest live node, and create a new node as a child of the fourth latest live node (if it exists) or the root of a new laminar tree (otherwise), and let the request of this node be that of the previous latest live node that has just been terminated.

We can apply Proposition 2.3 to the termination time of interval nodes in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) as well, which implies the following proposition.

Proposition 4.3.

At every time tt, the intervals I𝔫​(t)I_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) form a laminar family.

We apply tree terminology to nodes as follows: node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is said to be a parent, child, ancestor, descendant, or sibling of node 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} at time tt if I𝔫​(t)I_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is a parent, child, ancestor, descendant, or sibling of I𝔫′​(t)I_{\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}}(t) in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t), respectively. Denote by C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) the children of 𝔫\mathfrak{n} at time tt. We also define the roots of the trees to be siblings of each other. See Fig. 1 for an illustration of ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t).

It is easy to see that the following properties are maintained after every event.

Proposition 4.4.

Given an online algorithm that satisfies Property 4.2, for each time tt, the set of intervals I𝔫​(t)I_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) and ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) satisfy the following properties:

  1. 1.

    for every pending request qq, there is exactly one live node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} such that r⁡(𝔫)=qr(\mathfrak{n})=q;

  2. 2.

    the set of live nodes of pending requests forms a chain and corresponds to a rooted subpath in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t);

  3. 3.

    for each ii, the (i+1)(i+1)-th latest pending request’s live node is the parent of the ii-th latest pending request’s live node;

  4. 4.

    when a request qq arrives at time tt and it is not the only pending request, a new node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} such that r⁡(𝔫)=qr(\mathfrak{n})=q becomes a child of the previous latest pending request’s live node; if qq is the only pending request, then a new node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} such that r⁡(𝔫)=qr(\mathfrak{n})=q becomes a new root in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t).

Proposition 4.4 immediately implies that the corresponding requests of each node and its children satisfy the following ordering, which will be used later in the analysis.

Corollary 4.5.

For every node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} and 𝔫′∈C𝔫​(t)\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) at time tt when both 𝔫\mathfrak{n} and 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} are live, it holds that r⁡(𝔫)≺r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n})\prec r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}).

4.2 Description of Algorithm and Potential Function

In this part, we describe the sub-routine 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} for every vertex uu of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} is based on the previously defined laminar trees of interval nodes according to the requests that appear in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}. We first describe our algorithm in terms of the potential function Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}} for each node 𝔫\mathfrak{n}, and then define the potential function.

Odd and even states.

At a high level, our algorithm associates each node with a counter. At any point in time, 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} can either be in odd or even states, determined externally by the number of pending requests positioned at descendants of uu. If this number is even, then the latest node is active and all other nodes are frozen; otherwise if this number is odd, then the second latest node is active and all other nodes are frozen. Note that if uu is a leaf of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, then 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} is always in the even state and so the latest counter is active, which is the special case of a single-location metric as discussed in Section 1.1. The algorithm then matches either the corresponding requests of the latest two nodes or those of the second and the third latest nodes, based on the potential function. Based on those two states of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} and the corresponding rules of increasing the counter, we have the following definition:

Definition 4.6 (Critical parent and child).

At time tt, if 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} is in even state, then the latest two live nodes are said to be critical; otherwise the second and third latest live nodes are critical. More specifically, among two critical nodes, the earlier one is the critical parent and the later one is the critical child.

Since every request has a unique corresponding node at every moment when it is pending in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, the critical nodes correspond to two pending requests at every tt.

Algorithm description.

Our algorithm associates every node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} with a counter z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) that evolves over time as follows. Denote by z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) the value of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}’s counter at time tt and z𝔫′​(t)z^{\prime}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) to be its instantaneous increase. When a node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} arrives in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, its counter is initialized to zero, i.e., z𝔫​(au​(𝔫))=0z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))=0. At time tt, if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is the node that is active, then we increase its counter at the same rate as its corresponding request’s delay in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, i.e., the instantaneous counter increase is z𝔫′​(t)=fu,r⁡(𝔫)′​(t)z^{\prime}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)=f^{\prime}_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(t); every remaining node’s counter is frozen. Recall that we call the active node critical child and its parent critical parent (if its parent exists). We now specify the algorithm’s matching condition in terms of the counter values and the potential functions Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}}. Suppose we are at time tt and 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is the critical parent. The algorithm matches r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) with the request of the critical child when

Y𝔫​(t)≥12​z𝔫​(t).Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)\geq\frac{1}{2}z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t). (1)

And we call 𝔫\mathfrak{n} a primary node for every such match.

Remark 4.7.

We remark that the two failed attempts discussed in Section 1 can also be defined in this framework, by setting the potential function Yr​(t)Y_{r}(t) to be zr′​(t)z_{r^{\prime}}(t) (r′r^{\prime} is the current pending child) and ∑rj∈Cr​(t)zrj​(t)\sum_{r_{j}\in C_{r}(t)}z_{r_{j}}(t) respectively. In the single-location case, every request has a unique node at all times and so we can use the notation of requests to express nodes without ambiguity.

Potential function Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}}.

At a high level, the potential Y𝔫​(t)Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) of node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} at time tt depends on the counters of its children, and when those children were previously terminated when 𝔫\mathfrak{n} was not the critical parent.

The key insight underlying the potential function is as follows. Let 𝔫i≺u𝔫j\mathfrak{n}_{i}\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{j} be two children of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}, and 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} be a laminar optimal solution (Lemma 2.4) of the consolidated instance induced within TuT_{u}. If 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} matches some request qq that arrives before au​(𝔫i)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i}) with one that arrives after mu​(𝔫j)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j}), then we can charge the delay increase of r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) between au​(𝔫i)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i}) and mu​(𝔫j)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j}) to the match of qq made by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}. By laminarity, we can find distinct matches of 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} that induce a partition of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}’s children, which naturally suggests a charging scheme to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}; we prove this formally in Section 5.4.2. Since 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} and thus the partition is unknown to our online algorithm, we define the potential function to minimize among all.

Definition 4.8 (Canonical partitions).

Let 𝔫\mathfrak{n} be a node of ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) that is pending at time tt and 𝔫1≺u…≺u𝔫k\mathfrak{n}_{1}\prec_{u}\ldots\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{k} be its current children in C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t). A partition 𝒫𝔫\mathcal{P}_{\mathfrak{n}} of C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is contiguous if every part of the partition consists of consecutive children 𝔫i,𝔫i+1,…,𝔫j\mathfrak{n}_{i},\mathfrak{n}_{i+1},\ldots,\mathfrak{n}_{j}, and moreover, is canonical if {𝔫k}\{\mathfrak{n}_{k}\} is one of its parts.

Given a canonical partition 𝒫𝔫\mathcal{P}_{\mathfrak{n}} of C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t), its value is defined to be the sum of the values of its parts, where the value of part B𝔫={𝔫i,…,𝔫j}B_{\mathfrak{n}}=\{\mathfrak{n}_{i},\ldots,\mathfrak{n}_{j}\} is defined as follows:

v𝔫​(B𝔫)={fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(mu​(𝔫j))−fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(au​(𝔫i))if |B𝔫|>1;z𝔫j​(mu​(𝔫j))if |B𝔫|=1,v_{\mathfrak{n}}(B_{\mathfrak{n}})=\begin{cases}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j}))-f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i}))&\text{if $|B_{\mathfrak{n}}|>1$;}\\ z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j}))&\text{if $|B_{\mathfrak{n}}|=1$,}\end{cases} (2)

where mu​(𝔫j)m_{u}({\mathfrak{n}_{j}}) is assigned a tentative value of tt if 𝔫j\mathfrak{n}_{j} is still alive at time tt. In other words, if B𝔫B_{\mathfrak{n}} is a singleton, then its value is simply the counter value of its unique child. Otherwise, its value is the delay increase of r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) between the moments when 𝔫i\mathfrak{n}_{i} is added to the tree and when the last child 𝔫j\mathfrak{n}_{j} in B𝔫B_{\mathfrak{n}} is terminated.

Definition 4.9 (Potential function Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}}).

The potential function Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}} for node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is:

Y𝔫​(t):=min⁡∑B𝔫∈𝒫𝔫𝒫𝔫​ is a canonical partition of ​C𝔫​(t)⁡v𝔫​(B𝔫).Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t):=\min_{\mathcal{P}_{\mathfrak{n}}\text{ is a canonical partition of }C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)}\sum_{B_{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathfrak{n}}}v_{\mathfrak{n}}(B_{\mathfrak{n}}). (3)

Note that at any point in time, only the counter of the critical child can increase, and so only the potential of the critical parent can increase.

Remark 4.10.

We remark that the algorithm indeed matches all pending requests, provided that |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| is even and fr​(t)f_{r}(t) is unbounded for every r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}. Otherwise, suppose for contradiction that some requests remain unmatched forever, then they are all going to be promoted to the root of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Consider the latest two live nodes 𝔫≺u𝔫′\mathfrak{n}\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} in the instance of root uu, then 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is the critical parent and 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is the critical child, because there is zero request that is positioned at any other vertex. By definition, 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is the active node, so z𝔫′​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}}(t) tends to infinity, whereas z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) remains bounded because 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is frozen. Consequently, the matching condition must eventually be satisfied since Y𝔫​(t)≥z𝔫′​(t)Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)\geq z_{\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}}(t), contradicting the assumption that 𝔫\mathfrak{n} and 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} stay alive at the end.

5 Algorithm Analysis

We now analyze the competitive ratio of our algorithm and prove our main result Theorem 1.1.

Section overview.

In Section 5.1, we prove a key property of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} that the counters are geometrically decreasing along chains (Lemma 5.2). In Section 5.2, we define a set of primary nodes 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u} for each 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u} and show that the cost of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} is at most O⁡(1)O(1) times the total value of the counters of all 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u}’s (Lemma 5.7). In Section 5.3, we further prune the set of counters from 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u} into 𝒟up\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u} while only losing a constant factor of counter values (Proposition 5.11). Finally, in Section 5.4, we show that the total value of the counters of 𝒟up\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u} is at most O⁡(1)O(1) times 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, the optimal cost of the consolidated instance induced within TuT_{u} (Lemmas 5.21 and 5.26), and thus the desired competitive ratio of 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}.

Notation.

For brevity, for every 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, we write z𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}}, C𝔫C_{\mathfrak{n}}, and Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}} for the values of z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t), C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t), and Y𝔫​(t)Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) at time t=mu​(𝔫)t=m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), respectively (if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} stays alive at the end, then define mu​(𝔫)=∞m_{u}(\mathfrak{n})=\infty). Since the counter z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is frozen once 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is terminated, we have z𝔫=z𝔫​(mu​(𝔫))=z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}=z_{\mathfrak{n}}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))=z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) for every t≥mu​(𝔫)t\geq m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Likewise, C𝔫=C𝔫​(mu​(𝔫))=C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}=C_{\mathfrak{n}}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))=C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) and Y𝔫=Y𝔫​(mu​(𝔫))=Y𝔫​(t)Y_{\mathfrak{n}}=Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))=Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) for every t≥mu​(𝔫)t\geq m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). We write ℱu\mathcal{F}_{u} to mean ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) where tt tends to infinity.

5.1 Geometric Chain Property

We show that for every node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} in the forest ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t), its counter value is always at least twice its potential (Lemma 5.1) and then use it to prove that the counter values along chains are geometrically decreasing (Lemma 5.2).

Lemma 5.1.

For every vertex u∈Vu\in V and node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, z𝔫​(t)≥2​Y𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)\geq 2Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) at every time t≥au​(𝔫)t\geq a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), and z𝔫=2​Y𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}}=2Y_{\mathfrak{n}} if and only if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is the critical parent when it is terminated by 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}.

Proof.

Fix a node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} and define the function Y^𝔫​(t)=maxt′≤t⁡Y^𝔫​(t′)\widehat{Y}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)=\max_{t^{\prime}\leq t}\widehat{Y}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t^{\prime}). Since 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} terminates 𝔫\mathfrak{n} at time tt as a critical parent if Y𝔫​(t)≥12​z𝔫​(t)Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)\geq\frac{1}{2}z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t), to prove the lemma, it suffices to show that Y^𝔫​(t)\widehat{Y}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is continuous for every t≥au​(𝔫)t\geq a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}).

Suppose 𝔫\mathfrak{n} has |C𝔫|=k|C_{\mathfrak{n}}|=k children 𝔫1≺u…≺u𝔫k\mathfrak{n}_{1}\prec_{u}\ldots\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{k} and 𝒫𝔫∗​(t)\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is the canonical partition of minimum value. For each child 𝔫i\mathfrak{n}_{i}, since C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) does not vary between its arrival and the arrival of the next child 𝔫i+1\mathfrak{n}_{i+1}, we have that 𝒫𝔫∗​(t)\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) also does not vary until 𝔫i+1\mathfrak{n}_{i+1} arrives. Let 𝒫𝔫∗​(i)\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}(i) be the optimal partition of C𝔫​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) for t∈[au​(𝔫i),au​(𝔫i+1))t\in[a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i}),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i+1})). Since the counter value zqz_{q} is continuous for every node qq, we also have that Y𝔫​(t)Y_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) and Y^𝔫​(t)\widehat{Y}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) are continuous in the interval [au​(𝔫i),au​(𝔫i+1))[a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i}),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i+1})).

At t=au​(𝔫i+1)t=a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i+1}), the set of canonical partitions changes, which may cause a discontinuity in Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}}. Since the counter of 𝔫i+1\mathfrak{n}_{i+1} is 0 on arrival, the partition 𝒫𝔫∗​(i)∪{{𝔫i+1}}\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}(i)\cup\{\{\mathfrak{n}_{i+1}\}\} is a canonical partition of C𝔫​(au​(𝔫i+1))C_{\mathfrak{n}}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i+1})) with value equal to that of 𝒫𝔫∗​(i)\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}(i). Thus, if it is discontinuous at au​(𝔫i+1)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{i+1}), the potential can only decrease and so Y^𝔫​(t)\widehat{Y}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) remains continuous.

We conclude that Y^𝔫​(t)\widehat{Y}_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is continuous for every t≥au​(𝔫)t\geq a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), as desired. ∎

We now use Lemma 5.1 to prove that the counter values along chains are geometrically decreasing.

Lemma 5.2 (Geometric Chain Property).

Let 𝔫1≺u…≺u𝔫k\mathfrak{n}_{1}\prec_{u}\ldots\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{k} be all of the live nodes in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t). Then z𝔫j​(t)≥2​z𝔫j+1​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(t)\geq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}}(t) and z𝔫j≥2​z𝔫j+1z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}\geq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}} for every 1≤j≤k−11\leq j\leq k-1.

Proof.

Proposition 4.4 implies that 𝔫j+1\mathfrak{n}_{j+1} is the latest child of 𝔫j\mathfrak{n}_{j} among C𝔫j​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(t). By Lemma 5.1 and the fact that {𝔫j+1}\{\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}\} is a part in every canonical partition of C𝔫j​(t)C_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(t), we have that z𝔫j​(t)≥2​Y𝔫j​(t)≥2​z𝔫j+1​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(t)\geq 2Y_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(t)\geq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}}(t). This proves the first part of the lemma.

For the second part of the lemma, we first note that mu​(𝔫j)≥mu​(𝔫j+1)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j})\geq m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}) according to laminarity of node intervals. As a result, we apply the first part of the lemma to t=mu​(𝔫j+1)t=m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}) and get

z𝔫j​(mu​(𝔫j+1))≥2​z𝔫j+1​(mu​(𝔫j+1))=2​z𝔫j+1.z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}))\geq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}))=2z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}}.

Since counter values are nondecreasing with time, we get that z𝔫j≥z𝔫j​(mu​(𝔫j+1))≥2​z𝔫j+1z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}\geq z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}))\geq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}_{j+1}}. ∎

This property of decreasing geometric sequence will play an important role in allowing us to consider a subset of nodes and charge their counters to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, so as to avoid overcharging (Lemma 5.10).

5.2 Charging 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} to Counters

In this part, we show that we can use the total counter value of all primary requests as a proxy for the total cost of all 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s.

Definition 5.3 (Active and reluctant time).

For every 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, define its active time J𝔫J_{\mathfrak{n}} to be the set of times tt in which 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is active, its reluctant time J𝔫,1J_{\mathfrak{n},1} to be the set of times tt in which 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is the latest live node in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) yet inactive (𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} is in odd state). We also use J𝔫,0J_{\mathfrak{n},0} to denote the time when 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is neither active nor reluctant, or equivalently, J𝔫,0=I𝔫∖(J𝔫∪J𝔫,1)J_{\mathfrak{n},0}=I_{\mathfrak{n}}\setminus(J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n},1}).

For each node 𝔫\mathfrak{n}, we are going to relate the actual delay increase during interval I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} of request r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) to the final counter values of some nodes among different positions in 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Since every pending request in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} has a unique corresponding node interval at each moment, the total delays of all 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}’s can be bounded by the sum of delay increase during every node interval of its corresponding request, which allows us to analyse in the node-wise instead of request-wise way. Furthermore, for each node, we charge its reluctant time and the remaining part separately.

We first establish the following structural property, which shows that the interval J𝔫,0J_{\mathfrak{n},0} can be expressed as the union of JqJ_{q} and Jq,0J_{q,0} of every of its children qq.

Claim 5.4.

Let 𝔫\mathfrak{n} be a node. Then, for any two children q,q′q,q^{\prime} of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}, we have Iq∩Iq′=∅I_{q}\cap I_{q^{\prime}}=\varnothing. Moreover, J𝔫,0=∪q∈C𝔫(Jq∪Jq,0)J_{\mathfrak{n},0}=\cup_{q\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}}(J_{q}\cup J_{q,0}).

Proof.

Since qq and q′q^{\prime} are siblings, Proposition 4.4 implies that they cannot both be live at the same time, which in turn implies that Iq∩Iq′=∅I_{q}\cap I_{q^{\prime}}=\varnothing. According to our definition of two states of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} and reluctant time of nodes, J𝔫,0⊆∪q∈C𝔫IqJ_{\mathfrak{n},0}\subseteq\cup_{q\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}}I_{q}. Moreover, at each t∈Iq=Jq∪Jq,0∪Jq,1t\in I_{q}=J_{q}\cup J_{q,0}\cup J_{q,1} for a child q∈C𝔫q\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}: if t∈Jq,1t\in J_{q,1}, then counter z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is active and t∈J𝔫t\in J_{\mathfrak{n}}; if t∈Jq∪Jq,0t\in J_{q}\cup J_{q,0}, then 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is neither active nor reluctant, and so t∈J𝔫,0t\in J_{\mathfrak{n},0}. As a result, J𝔫,0=∪q∈C𝔫(Jq∪Jq,0)J_{\mathfrak{n},0}=\cup_{q\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}}(J_{q}\cup J_{q,0}). ∎

Lemma 5.5.

For every vertex u∈Vu\in V and 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, we have z𝔫≤fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫∪J𝔫,0)≤2​z𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n},0})\leq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}}.

Proof.

We start with the base case: when I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} is a leaf in ℱu\mathcal{F}_{u}. In this case, C𝔫=∅C_{\mathfrak{n}}=\varnothing, and so by Claim 5.4, J𝔫,0=∅J_{\mathfrak{n},0}=\varnothing. Thus, z𝔫=fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫∪J𝔫,0)z_{\mathfrak{n}}=f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n},0}).

By Claim 5.4, we have fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫∪J𝔫,0)=z𝔫+∑𝔫j∈C𝔫fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫j∪J𝔫j,0)f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n},0})=z_{\mathfrak{n}}+\sum_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j},0}). Suppose C𝔫C_{\mathfrak{n}} consists of 𝔫1≺u…≺u𝔫k\mathfrak{n}_{1}\prec_{u}\ldots\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{k} and 𝒫𝔫∗\mathcal{P}_{\mathfrak{n}}^{*} is the canonical partition of C𝔫C_{\mathfrak{n}} such that ∑B𝔫∈𝒫𝔫∗v𝔫​(B𝔫)=Y𝔫\sum_{B_{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}}v_{\mathfrak{n}}(B_{\mathfrak{n}})=Y_{\mathfrak{n}}, then we have ∑𝔫j∈C𝔫fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫j∪J𝔫j,0)=∑B𝔫∈𝒫𝔫∗∑𝔫j∈B𝔫fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫j∪J𝔫j,0)\sum_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j},0})=\sum_{B_{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}\in B_{\mathfrak{n}}}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j},0}). ∑𝔫j∈B𝔫fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫j∪J𝔫j,0)≤fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(mu​(𝔫b2))−fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(au​(𝔫b1))=v𝔫​(B𝔫).\sum_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}\in B_{\mathfrak{n}}}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j},0})\leq f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{b_{2}}))-f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}_{b_{1}}))=v_{\mathfrak{n}}(B_{\mathfrak{n}}).

fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫b∪J𝔫b,0)≤fu,r⁡(𝔫b)​(J𝔫b∪J𝔫b,0)≤2​z𝔫b=2​v𝔫​(B𝔫),f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}_{b}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n}_{b},0})\leq f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n}_{b})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}_{b}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n}_{b},0})\leq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}_{b}}=2v_{\mathfrak{n}}(B_{\mathfrak{n}}),
