fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫∪J𝔫,0)\displaystyle f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n},0}) =z𝔫+∑B𝔫∈𝒫𝔫∗∑𝔫j∈B𝔫fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫j∪J𝔫j,0)\displaystyle=z_{\mathfrak{n}}+\sum_{B_{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}\in B_{\mathfrak{n}}}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n}_{j},0})
≤z𝔫+2​∑B𝔫∈𝒫𝔫∗v𝔫​(B𝔫)\displaystyle\leq z_{\mathfrak{n}}+2\sum_{B_{\mathfrak{n}}\in\mathcal{P}^{*}_{\mathfrak{n}}}v_{\mathfrak{n}}(B_{\mathfrak{n}})
=z𝔫+2​Y𝔫≤2​z𝔫,\displaystyle=z_{\mathfrak{n}}+2Y_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 2z_{\mathfrak{n}},

where the last inequality holds by Lemma 5.1. ∎

Next we consider the delay increase during J𝔫,1J_{\mathfrak{n},1} when 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is reluctant. In this part, we want to avoid nodes 𝔫\mathfrak{n} such that: 𝔫∈ℱu​(t)\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) but r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) is not positioned at uu, because they do not actually represent their requests’ positions or contribute to positive counter increase. At time tt, we call a live node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} a valid node if r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) is a pending request positioned at uu. We then show that when a valid node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is reluctant at time tt, we can always find another valid node that is not reluctant at some moment within the subtree TuT_{u} to charge the instantaneous delay increase of r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) to. Moreover, the total charge a valid node that is not reluctant at a given moment can receive is no more than HH times its instantaneous delay increase. In summary, the following lemma gives us an upper bound of the total delay incurred by every node when it is reluctant, expressed in terms of the total counter values.

Lemma 5.6.

∑u∈V∑𝔫∈𝒩ufu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫,1)≤4​(H−1)​∑u∈V∑𝔫∈𝒩uz𝔫\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n},1})\leq 4(H-1)\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}.

Proof.

We will define a pair of mappings (ζ,χ)(\zeta,\chi) on all tuples (𝔫,t)(\mathfrak{n},t) of valid node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} and time tt such that 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is reluctant at tt. Furthermore, ζ⁡(𝔫,t)\zeta(\mathfrak{n},t) is a tuple (𝔫′,t′)(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime}) such that 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is a valid node at t′t^{\prime}, and χ⁡(𝔫,t)\chi(\mathfrak{n},t) is a value such that fr⁡(𝔫)′​(t)≤χ⁡(𝔫,t)​fr⁡(𝔫′)′​(t′)f_{r(\mathfrak{n})}^{\prime}(t)\leq\chi(\mathfrak{n},t)f^{\prime}_{r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})}(t^{\prime}).

Now we show how to define the mapping. Given a valid reluctant 𝔫\mathfrak{n} at time tt whose position is uu, the total number of requests positioned at descendants of uu is odd. As a result, there is a descendant u′u^{\prime} of uu such that: at time tt, there is at least one request positioned at u′u^{\prime} and the total number of requests positioned with Tu′T_{u^{\prime}} is odd, while no request is positioned at any vertex on the path between uu and u′u^{\prime}. If there is at least one valid active node at u′u^{\prime}, then define ζ⁡(𝔫,t)=(𝔫′,t)\zeta(\mathfrak{n},t)=(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t) and χ⁡(𝔫,t)=1\chi(\mathfrak{n},t)=1. Otherwise, we show that there must be a request qq positioned at u′u^{\prime} that does not have a live node: (Case 1) if an odd number of requests are positioned at u′u^{\prime}, then 𝖠𝖫𝖦u′\mathsf{ALG}_{u^{\prime}} is in even state and so as long as there exists at least one valid node, the latest one must be active; (Case 2) if an even number (at least two) of requests are positioned at u′u^{\prime}, then 𝖠𝖫𝖦u′\mathsf{ALG}_{u^{\prime}} is in odd state and so the second latest live (and valid) node is active if every request positioned at u′u^{\prime} has a live node. As a result, 𝖠𝖫𝖦u′\mathsf{ALG}_{u^{\prime}} must have matched qq with a request q′≺qq^{\prime}\prec q such that q′q^{\prime} has already been promoted to the parent of u′u^{\prime} before this match. In this case, let t′t^{\prime} be the moment that fq′​(t′)=fq​(t)f_{q^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})=f_{q}(t) (t′t^{\prime} is unique according to our bijection assumption of every request’s delay), then q′q^{\prime} has a unique valid node 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} in ℱu′​(t′)\mathcal{F}_{u^{\prime}}(t^{\prime}). We define ζ⁡(𝔫,t)=(𝔫′,t′)\zeta(\mathfrak{n},t)=(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime}) and χ⁡(𝔫,t)=fq′​(t)fq′′​(t′)\chi(\mathfrak{n},t)=\frac{f^{\prime}_{q}(t)}{f^{\prime}_{q^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})}. It is easy to see that fr⁡(𝔫)′​(t)≤χ⁡(𝔫,t)​fr⁡(𝔫′)′​(t′)f^{\prime}_{r(\mathfrak{n})}(t)\leq\chi(\mathfrak{n},t)f^{\prime}_{r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})}(t^{\prime}) holds as fr⁡(𝔫)′​(t)≤fq′​(t)f_{r(\mathfrak{n})}^{\prime}(t)\leq f^{\prime}_{q}(t) (Observation 3.2), and we have the local derivative d​t′d​t=χ⁡(𝔫,t)\frac{dt^{\prime}}{dt}=\chi(\mathfrak{n},t).

From the above paragraph, ζ⁡(𝔫,t)\zeta(\mathfrak{n},t) is well-defined for every reluctant valid node at tt. Moreover, if (𝔫′,t′)=ζ⁡(𝔫,t)(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime})=\zeta(\mathfrak{n},t), then the position of 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is a descendant of that of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}. Because there is no reluctant node at any leaf vertex, for every reluctant 𝔫\mathfrak{n} at time tt, there exist k≤H−1k\leq H-1 and ζk​(𝔫,t)=(𝔫′,t′)\zeta^{k}(\mathfrak{n},t)=(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime}) such that 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is not a reluctant node at time t′t^{\prime}. We define 𝒢⁡(𝔫,t)=(𝔫′,t′)\mathcal{G}(\mathfrak{n},t)=(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime}) and Ψ⁡(𝔫,t)=Πℓ=0k−1​χ​(ζℓ​(𝔫,t))\Psi(\mathfrak{n},t)=\Pi_{\ell=0}^{k-1}\chi(\zeta^{\ell}(\mathfrak{n},t)), then fr⁡(𝔫)′​(t)≤Ψ⁡(𝔫,t)​fr⁡(𝔫′)′​(t′)f_{r(\mathfrak{n})}^{\prime}(t)\leq\Psi(\mathfrak{n},t)f^{\prime}_{r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})}(t^{\prime}) and so we charge the delay increase of fr⁡(𝔫)′​(t)​d​tf^{\prime}_{r(\mathfrak{n})}(t)dt to fr⁡(𝔫′)′​(t′)​d​t′f^{\prime}_{r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})}(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime} by the substitution d​t′=Ψ⁡(𝔫,t)​d​tdt^{\prime}=\Psi(\mathfrak{n},t)dt derived from the chain rule of differentiation.

Next we bound the number of tuples (𝔫,t)(\mathfrak{n},t) such that 𝒢⁡(𝔫,t)=(𝔫′,t′)\mathcal{G}(\mathfrak{n},t)=(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime}) for every valid non-reluctant node 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} at time t′t^{\prime}. |ζ−1​(𝔫′,t′)|≤2|\zeta^{-1}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime})|\leq 2 according to the two cases that we define ζ⁡(𝔫,t)\zeta(\mathfrak{n},t). For every reluctant node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} at time tt, |ζ−1​(𝔫,t)||\zeta^{-1}(\mathfrak{n},t)| is at most one, because in the first case the function value (𝔫,t)(\mathfrak{n},t) has to be an active node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} at time tt. As a result, there are at most two different chains beginning at (𝔫′,t′)(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime}) where the next element in the chain is a pre-image of the previous one, and each chain is of length no more than HH (including (𝔫′,t′)(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime}) itself). Therefore, |𝒢−1​(𝔫′,t′)|=∑k=1H−1|ζ−k​(𝔫′,t′)|≤2​(H−1)|\mathcal{G}^{-1}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime})|=\sum_{k=1}^{H-1}|\zeta^{-k}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime},t^{\prime})|\leq 2(H-1).

We conclude that the total charge is no more than 2​(H−1)​∑u∈V∑𝔫∈𝒩ufu,r⁡(𝔫)​(J𝔫∪J𝔫,0)2(H-1)\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}}f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cup J_{\mathfrak{n},0}), which is no more than 4​(H−1)​∑u∈V∑𝔫∈𝒩uz𝔫4(H-1)\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}}z_{\mathfrak{n}} according to Lemma 5.5. ∎

Combined with Lemma 5.5, it holds that ∑u∈V𝖠𝖫𝖦u≤(4​H−2)​∑u∈V∑𝔫∈𝒩uz𝔫\sum_{u\in V}\mathsf{ALG}_{u}\leq(4H-2)\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}.

Next, we show that it suffices to consider the counters of primary nodes. Let 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u} denote the set of primary nodes in 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u}: we have previously defined every critical parent node when a match happens to be a primary node, here we complement it by also including the earliest node among all that stay alive at the end (if there is any). By applying Lemma 5.2 to nodes that are terminated at the same moment and nodes that stay alive at the end, it is easy to see that we can use 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u} to represent node counters in 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u} while only losing a factor of 22. Thus, we can bound the cost of all single-location subroutines by the counters of primary nodes, up to a constant:

Lemma 5.7 (Charging to Counters).

∑u∈V𝖠𝖫𝖦u≤(8​H−4)​∑u∈V∑𝔫∈𝒟uz𝔫\sum_{u\in V}\mathsf{ALG}_{u}\leq(8H-4)\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}_{u}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}.

5.3 Pruning Counters

We now fix a vertex uu of 𝒯\mathcal{T} and prune the set of counters from 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u} based on 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}’s matching Mu∗M^{*}_{u}, to finally define the desired set 𝒟up\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u} that we will charge to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

For the case where there is one request rr unmatched by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} because |ℛu||\mathcal{R}_{u}| is odd, we define a request r∞r_{\infty} such that a⁡(r∞)=∞a(r_{\infty})=\infty and its delay is zero, and include (r,r∞)∈Mu∗(r,r_{\infty})\in M^{*}_{u}. For every time interval II, we say that r∞∈Ir_{\infty}\in I if II is right-unbounded. In the definitions and analysis hereafter (e.g. Definitions 5.8 and 5.19) we regard r∞r_{\infty} as a request in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u} and (r,r∞)(r,r_{\infty}) as a match made by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

In the following analysis and definitions, for an interval I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}}, if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is at a leaf vertex uu and so a⁡(r⁡(𝔫))=au​(𝔫)a(r(\mathfrak{n}))=a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), then we do not include the request r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) itself when we consider Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}). Otherwise, we assume without loss of generality that no request arrival occurs at the exact moment au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}).

Definition 5.8 (Preempted nodes and intervals).

A node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} and its interval I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} are said to be left-preempted (or right-preempted, resp.) if there exists a request r∈ℛur\in\mathcal{R}_{u} that arrives during I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} that 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} matches with a request qq with a​(q)<au​(𝔫)a(q)<a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) (or a​(q)>mu​(𝔫)a(q)>m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), resp.).

Note that a node may be simultaneously left- and right-preempted.

Definition 5.9 (Left- and right-equivalent requests).

For every 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted, define hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) to be the latest arrival in Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) that is matched by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} to a request that arrives before au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Similarly, if it is right-preempted, define hright​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{right}}(\mathfrak{n}) to be the earliest in Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) that is matched by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} to a request that arrives after mu​(𝔫)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Nodes 𝔫1,𝔫2\mathfrak{n}_{1},\mathfrak{n}_{2} are said to be left-equivalent if hleft​(𝔫1)=hleft​(𝔫2)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}_{1})=h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}_{2}), and right-equivalent if hright​(𝔫1)=hright​(𝔫2)h^{\mathrm{right}}(\mathfrak{n}_{1})=h^{\mathrm{right}}(\mathfrak{n}_{2}).

Later, we will charge portions of the counter values to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} based on hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) and hright​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{right}}(\mathfrak{n}). This may lead to overcharging if multiple requests belong to the same left- or right-equivalence class. The following lemma allows us to restrict our attention to a pruned subset in which no two requests are left- or right-equivalent, while losing only a constant factor.

Lemma 5.10.

For any set of nodes 𝒮⊆𝒩u\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{N}_{u}, there exists a subset 𝒮p⊆𝒮\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}}\subseteq\mathcal{S} such that ∑𝔫∈𝒮z𝔫≤4​∑𝔫∈𝒮pz𝔫\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{S}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 4\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}}}z_{\mathfrak{n}} and no two nodes in 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}} are left-equivalent or right-equivalent.

Proof.

First, observe that if two nodes 𝔫1,𝔫2\mathfrak{n}_{1},\mathfrak{n}_{2} are left-equivalent or right-equivalent, then either I𝔫1⊇I𝔫2I_{\mathfrak{n}_{1}}\supseteq I_{\mathfrak{n}_{2}} or I𝔫1⊆I𝔫2I_{\mathfrak{n}_{1}}\subseteq I_{\mathfrak{n}_{2}}. In particular, a left-equivalence (or right-equivalence) class QQ forms a chain, and thus Lemma 5.2 implies that ∑𝔫∈Qz𝔫≤2​max𝔫∈Q​z𝔫\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in Q}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 2\max_{\mathfrak{n}\in Q}z_{\mathfrak{n}}.

Given any 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we obtain 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}} in two stages. Initially, let 𝒮p=𝒮\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}}=\mathcal{S}. In the first stage, for each left-equivalence class in 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}}, we remove from 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}} all nodes except the one with the highest counter value. In the second stage, we apply the same pruning procedure to each right-equivalence class among the remaining nodes in 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}}.

By the above argument, the total counter value of 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}} decreases by a factor of at most 22 in each stage. Hence, ∑𝔫∈𝒮z𝔫≤4​∑𝔫∈𝒮pz𝔫\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{S}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 4\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{p}}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}. ∎

Combining Lemmas 5.10 and 5.7, we immediately get the following:

Proposition 5.11.

There is a set of nodes 𝒟up⊆𝒟u\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{u} such that the total cost of all virtual algorithms ∑u∈V𝖠𝖫𝖦u≤(32​H−16)​∑u∈V∑𝔫∈𝒟upz𝔫\sum_{u\in V}\mathsf{ALG}_{u}\leq(32H-16)\sum_{u\in V}\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u}}z_{\mathfrak{n}} and no two nodes in 𝒟up\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u} are left-equivalent or right-equivalent.

5.4 Charging Counters to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}

Fix u∈Vu\in V. Let 𝒟up\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u} be the pruned set of primary nodes guaranteed by Proposition 5.11. In the remainder of this section, we show that ∑𝔫∈𝒟upz𝔫≤O⁡(1)⋅𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq O(1)\cdot\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} via a charging scheme. We first define odd and even subintervals which lets us partition nodes into two groups: aligned and misaligned, based on the state of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} right after their arrivals as well as how 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} matches requests that arrive during those intervals. In Section 5.4.1, we show that the total counter value of aligned nodes is at most O⁡(1)⋅𝖮𝖯𝖳^uO(1)\cdot\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}. Handling the misaligned nodes is significantly more challenging, and is where the potential function becomes necessary. In Section 5.4.2, we charge part of the counters to aligned nodes and some directly to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

Definition 5.12 (Odd and even nodes).

For every 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, consider the state of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} right after au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) when 𝔫\mathfrak{n} arrives: we say that 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd (or even, resp.) if 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} is in odd (or even, resp.) state.

Note that if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is at a leaf vertex, then it is always even, which is a special case where the algorithm runs on a single-location metric.

Odd and even subintervals.

We use I𝔫oddI_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{odd}} to denote all time t∈I𝔫t\in I_{\mathfrak{n}} by which an odd number of requests from Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) have arrived and similarly define I𝔫evenI_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{even}}. We get that whenever the counter of node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is active at tt, it must hold that t∈I𝔫oddt\in I^{\mathrm{odd}}_{\mathfrak{n}} if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd and t∈I𝔫event\in I^{\mathrm{even}}_{\mathfrak{n}} if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (Lemma 5.15). As a result, when we charge z𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, we want to find a request that is pending during I𝔫oddI^{\mathrm{odd}}_{\mathfrak{n}} or I𝔫evenI^{\mathrm{even}}_{\mathfrak{n}} depending on the state of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} right after au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), and we will discuss different cases depending on whether such a request can be found.

Definition 5.13 (I𝔫odd,I𝔫evenI_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{odd}},I_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{even}}).

Let 𝔫\mathfrak{n} be a node in 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u} and k=|Ru​(I𝔫)|k=|R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}})|, the number of requests that arrive during time interval I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} within subtree TuT_{u}. For each 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, let rjr_{j} be the jj-th earliest request of Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) and bjb_{j} be its arrival time (define b0b_{0} to be au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})). Moreover, define a request rjr_{j} to be 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd if jj is odd and 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even otherwise. The arrival times au​(𝔫)=b0<b1<…<bk<mu​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})=b_{0}<b_{1}<\ldots<b_{k}<m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) partition I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} into odd and even subintervals as follows: for j<kj<k, the jj-th subinterval is [bj,bj+1)[b_{j},b_{j+1}); the final subinterval is [bk,mu​(𝔫))[b_{k},m_{u}(\mathfrak{n})). Denote by I𝔫oddI_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{odd}} and I𝔫evenI_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{even}} the union of the jj-th subintervals for odd jj and even jj, respectively.

In the remainder of the analysis, when we compare 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} and its node counters and intervals against all requests in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u}, we regard those that have not been promoted to uu as requests under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} as well. For requests that have not been promoted to uu, we regard their matching status under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} as per whether they are pending or have been matched by the actual algorithm 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}. After they are promoted to uu, we regard their matching status under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} as per whether they have been matched in the virtual instance ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, rather than whether they have actually been matched by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}. According to the mechanism of each 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} and Corollary 4.5, the counter of a live node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is only active when the number of pending requests under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} that arrive later than r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) is even. The next lemma derived from basic properties of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} and the laminar forest relates its parity to the arrivals of requests in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u}.

Lemma 5.14.

For every 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, during I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}}, the parity of the number of pending requests under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} that arrive after r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) only changes when a new request in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u} arrives.

Proof.

It is easy to see the parity in question does not change when a request is promoted to a new vertex within TuT_{u}, or when two requests that are positioned at some descendant of uu are matched by 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG}. If it is changed by a match made by 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u}, then 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} must have matched a pair of requests (q,q′)(q,q^{\prime}) that q≺r⁡(𝔫)≺q′q\prec r(\mathfrak{n})\prec q^{\prime}. Assume this happens at time tt, then 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is between nodes of qq and q′q^{\prime} on the path of live nodes in ℱu​(t)\mathcal{F}_{u}(t) (Proposition 4.4), a contradiction to Property 4.2. ∎

Now we come to the key property that links the counter increase to the parity of subintervals.

Lemma 5.15.

For every node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}, we have J𝔫⊆I𝔫oddJ_{\mathfrak{n}}\subseteq I_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{odd}} if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd and J𝔫⊆I𝔫evenJ_{\mathfrak{n}}\subseteq I_{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathrm{even}} if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even.

Proof.

We prove the case that 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd, and the other case can be shown analogously. At each moment t∈J𝔫t\in J_{\mathfrak{n}}, there are even number of pending requests in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u} under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} that arrive after r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}). Because 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd, the parity in question is odd at au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Furthermore, it only changes when a new request in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u} arrives (Lemma 5.14), and so for every moment tt when it is even, tt must be in I𝔫oddI^{\mathrm{odd}}_{\mathfrak{n}}, hence our claim. ∎

We now consider how the requests in Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) are matched by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, which will be important for our charging scheme.

Definition 5.16 (Aligned and misaligned nodes).

A node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} is aligned if: hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even, resp.) and 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.); or, if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd and not left-preempted. Otherwise 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is misaligned. Let 𝒟u,ap\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a} and 𝒟u,mp\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m} be the sets of aligned and misaligned nodes in 𝒟up\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u}, respectively.

We need to be cautious with the primary node (at most one) that stays alive at the end, because it is not matched as a critical parent and hence we cannot use its potential to charge, as what we do to misaligned primary nodes in Section 5.4.2. Luckily, we show that such a primary node must be aligned and so we can directly charge z𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} as in Section 5.4.1, without reliance on Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}}.

We first prove a property that will be used for 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, as it is laminar.

Lemma 5.17.

Let (M,m)(M,m) be a laminar solution. Then, for every match (r,r′)∈M(r,r^{\prime})\in M, the number of requests qq such that r≺q≺r′r\prec q\prec r^{\prime} is even.

Proof.

Because a laminar solution always matches the latest two pending requests at the time, when (r,r′)(r,r^{\prime}) is matched, all requests that arrive between rr and r′r^{\prime} have all been matched. Any request qq that r≺q≺r′r\prec q\prec r^{\prime} cannot be matched with any request q′q^{\prime} such that q′≺rq^{\prime}\prec r or q′≻r′q^{\prime}\succ r^{\prime} when rr and r′r^{\prime} are both unmatched, otherwise it is a violation of the laminar property. As a result, all requests that arrive between rr and r′r^{\prime} are matched into pairs by (M,m)(M,m), and thus the number of such requests must be even. ∎

Lemma 5.18.

If 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} is the primary node that stays alive at the end, then 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is aligned.

Proof.

Because 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} is the primary node that stays alive at the end, all requests that arrive before r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) are: either never promoted to uu, or matched in ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} before au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Let k1k_{1} be the number of requests that arrive before r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}), k2k_{2} be the number of requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫)),au​(𝔫)](a(r(\mathfrak{n})),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})], k3k_{3} be the number of requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫)),au​(𝔫)](a(r(\mathfrak{n})),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})] and are unmatched under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} at au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). According to the mechanism of 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} and Lemma 5.14, for requests that arrive before r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}): under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}, either they are matched with each other, or they can only be matched with requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫)),au​(𝔫)](a(r(\mathfrak{n})),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})] by the moment au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Therefore, k1−k2k_{1}-k_{2} has the same parity as k3k_{3}, and 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd (or even, resp.) if and only if k3k_{3} is odd (or even, resp.); this happens if and only if k1+k2+1k_{1}+k_{2}+1, the number of requests that arrive before au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) (including r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n})), is even (or odd, resp.). By laminarity of 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} and Lemma 5.17, when hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) exists, because ρ​(hleft​(𝔫))\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})) is at an odd position among all requests in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u}, hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) is at an even position. If the number of requests that arrive before au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) is even (or odd, resp.), then hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd, resp.). If hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) does not exist, then k1+k2+1k_{1}+k_{2}+1 must be even and so 𝔫\mathfrak{n} must be odd. In summary, 𝔫\mathfrak{n} must be aligned. ∎

We introduce the following notation to express the structure of 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} as well as its cost.

Definition 5.19.

For every r∈ℛur\in\mathcal{R}_{u} that is matched by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, let ρ⁡(r)\rho(r) denote the request that 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} matches rr with, and c⁡(r)c(r) denote the delay incurred by a request rr under 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} if ρ⁡(r)≻r\rho(r)\succ r or the delay incurred by ρ⁡(r)\rho(r) if r≻ρ⁡(r)r\succ\rho(r), both under 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

Observe that 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u=∑r∈ℛu:r≺ρ⁡(r)c(r)=∑r∈ℛu:r≻ρ⁡(r)c(r)\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{u}:r\prec\rho(r)}c(r)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{u}:r\succ\rho(r)}c(r).

Dividing I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} and J𝔫J_{\mathfrak{n}} into two parts.

If 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted, let qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) be the first request that arrives after hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}); otherwise, define qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) to be the first request that arrives after au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). We divide I𝔫=[au​(𝔫),mu​(𝔫))I_{\mathfrak{n}}=[a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}),m_{u}(\mathfrak{n})) into two parts: I𝔫left=[au​(𝔫),a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)))I^{\mathrm{left}}_{\mathfrak{n}}=[a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}),a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))) and I𝔫right=[a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)),mu​(𝔫))I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}=[a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})),m_{u}(\mathfrak{n})) (I𝔫right=∅I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}=\varnothing if qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) arrives after mu​(𝔫)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) or does not exist). Observe that Ru​(I𝔫left)R_{u}(I^{\mathrm{left}}_{\mathfrak{n}}) is the subset of Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) that arrive before qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) (including hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted). Moreover, if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is not left-preempted, then all requests in Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) arrive during I𝔫rightI^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}; if qleft​(𝔫)∉Ru​(I𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})\notin R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) or qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) does not exist, then all requests in Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) arrive during I𝔫leftI^{\mathrm{left}}_{\mathfrak{n}}. We also divide J𝔫J_{\mathfrak{n}} into J𝔫left=J𝔫∩I𝔫leftJ^{\mathrm{left}}_{\mathfrak{n}}=J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cap I^{\mathrm{left}}_{\mathfrak{n}} and J𝔫right=J𝔫∩I𝔫rightJ^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}=J_{\mathfrak{n}}\cap I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}.

Claim 5.20.

𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} matches every request in Ru​(I𝔫right)R_{u}(I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}) to one that arrives no earlier than qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}).

Proof.

By definition of left-preemption, the claim is true if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is not left-preempted. Suppose 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted. Since every request of Ru​(I𝔫right)R_{u}(I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}) arrives after hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}), by definition of hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}), no request in Ru​(I𝔫right)R_{u}(I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}) is matched by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} to a request that arrives earlier than au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Moreover, 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} matches hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) to a request that arrives earlier than au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Thus, by laminarity, no request in Ru​(I𝔫right)R_{u}(I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}) can be matched with a request in Ru​(I𝔫left)R_{u}(I^{\mathrm{left}}_{\mathfrak{n}}) either. This gives us the claim. ∎

5.4.1 Charging aligned counters 𝒟u,ap\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}

Recall that node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is aligned if hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even, resp.) and 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.), or if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd and not left-preempted. In this subsection, we are going to prove a stronger statement. Let 𝒩u,a\mathcal{N}_{u,a} be the set of all aligned nodes in 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u} and 𝒩u,ap\mathcal{N}_{u,a}^{\mathrm{p}} be the pruned subset of it by applying Lemma 5.10 to 𝒩u,a\mathcal{N}_{u,a}, and so ∑𝔫∈𝒩u,az𝔫≤4​∑𝔫∈𝒩u,apz𝔫\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u,a}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 4\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u,a}^{\mathrm{p}}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}. We will charge 𝒩u,ap\mathcal{N}_{u,a}^{\mathrm{p}} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, which then provides an upper bound of 𝒩u,a\mathcal{N}_{u,a} as well as 𝒟u,ap\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a} since 𝒟u,ap⊆𝒩u,a\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a}\subseteq\mathcal{N}_{u,a}. Our main lemma is the following:

Lemma 5.21 (Bounding Aligned Counters).

∑𝔫∈𝒟u,apz𝔫≤8​𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}_{u,a}^{\mathrm{p}}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 8\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

High level overview.

The key property of an aligned node 𝔫\mathfrak{n} that is odd (or even, resp.) is that, for every odd (or even, resp.) subinterval of I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} from qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) onwards, 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} has at least one request in Ru​(I𝔫right)R_{u}(I^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}) that is pending for the entire subinterval. Since 𝔫\mathfrak{n} can only be active during odd (or even,resp.) subintervals if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd (or even, resp.), for t≥a⁡(qleft​(𝔫))t\geq a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})), we can charge the instantaneous delay of r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) when 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is active to the instantaneous delay of a pending request in 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}. Since we can find such a pending request in Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}), its instantaneous delay increase must always be at least that of r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) by noncrossing delays, and thus the instantaneous charging argument works. We can charge the remaining portion of the counter value, i.e., the part up till a​(qleft​(𝔫))a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})), to c​(hleft​(𝔫))c(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})), whose value is at least fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))−fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(au​(𝔫))f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))-f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})) no matter whether ρ​(hleft​(𝔫))\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})) arrives before or after r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}), also by properties of noncrossing delays, and thus at least z𝔫​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))).

Claim 5.22.

Let 𝔫\mathfrak{n} be an aligned node such that qleft​(𝔫)∈Ru​(I𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})\in R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}). If 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd (or even, resp.), then for every odd (or even, resp.) subinterval I=[bj,bj+1)I=[b_{j},b_{j+1}) of I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} with bj≥a⁡(qleft​(𝔫))b_{j}\geq a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})), there exists a request g𝔫​(t)⪰r​(𝔫)g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)\succeq r(\mathfrak{n}) that is pending in 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} for every t∈It\in I.

Proof.

Let SS be the set of requests that arrive in [a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)),bj][a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})),b_{j}]. Since 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is aligned, regardless of whether 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted or not, qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even, resp.) if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd (or even, resp.). Thus, |S||S| is odd in both cases. By Claim 5.20, 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} matches none of SS to requests earlier than a​(qleft​(𝔫))a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})). Since the next request arrives at time bj+1b_{j+1}, 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} must keep some request of SS pending during the subinterval II. ∎

Lemma 5.23.

Let 𝔫\mathfrak{n} be an aligned node. If 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted, then z𝔫≤c⁡(hleft​(𝔫))+∫J𝔫rightf^g𝔫​(t)′​(t)​𝑑tz_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq c(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))+\int_{J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}\hat{f}^{\prime}_{g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)}(t)dt; otherwise, z𝔫≤∫J𝔫rightf^g𝔫​(t)′​(t)​𝑑tz_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq\int_{J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}\hat{f}^{\prime}_{g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)}(t)dt.

Proof.

We have

z𝔫=∫J𝔫leftfu,r⁡(𝔫)′​(t)​𝑑t+∫J𝔫rightfu,r⁡(𝔫)′​(t)​𝑑t=z𝔫​(a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)))+∫J𝔫rightfu,r⁡(𝔫)′​(t)​𝑑t.z_{\mathfrak{n}}=\int_{J^{\mathrm{left}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}f^{\prime}_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(t)dt+\int_{J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}f^{\prime}_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(t)dt=z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))+\int_{J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}f^{\prime}_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(t)dt.

We now bound the two terms separately. According to Lemmas 5.15 and 5.22, g𝔫​(t)g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is defined for every t∈J𝔫rightt\in J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}. The fact that g𝔫​(t)⪰r​(𝔫)g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)\succeq r(\mathfrak{n}) and the noncrossing property of the consolidated instance imply the following bound on the integral: ∫J𝔫rightfu,r⁡(𝔫)′​(t)​𝑑t=∫J𝔫rightf^r⁡(𝔫)′​(t)​𝑑t≤∫J𝔫rightf^g𝔫​(t)′​(t)​𝑑t\int_{J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}f^{\prime}_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(t)dt=\int_{J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}\hat{f}^{\prime}_{r(\mathfrak{n})}(t)dt\leq\int_{J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}}\hat{f}^{\prime}_{g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)}(t)dt.

It remains to bound z𝔫​(a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)))z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))). If 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is not left-preempted, then 𝔫\mathfrak{n} must be odd and so z𝔫​(t)z_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) is frozen before the arrival of qleft​(𝔫)q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}), we are done. Otherwise, hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even, resp.) and 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is only active during even (or odd, resp.) subintervals if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.), we have that z𝔫​(a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)))=z𝔫​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))=z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))). The arrival time of ρ​(hleft​(𝔫))\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})) is earlier than au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), and there are two cases: ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))⪯r⁡(𝔫)\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))\preceq r(\mathfrak{n}), or r⁡(𝔫)≺ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))r(\mathfrak{n})\prec\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})). If ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))⪯r⁡(𝔫)\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))\preceq r(\mathfrak{n}), then

z𝔫​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))≤fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))≤f^r⁡(𝔫)​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))≤f^ρ​(hleft​(𝔫))​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))=c⁡(hleft​(𝔫)),z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))\leq f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))\leq\hat{f}_{r(\mathfrak{n})}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))\leq\hat{f}_{\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))=c(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})),

according to the noncrossing property that the total delay of a later request is no more than that of an earlier one. If r⁡(𝔫)≺ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))r(\mathfrak{n})\prec\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})), then

z𝔫​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))\displaystyle z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))) ≤fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))−fu,r⁡(𝔫)​(au​(𝔫))\displaystyle\leq f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))-f_{u,r(\mathfrak{n})}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))
=f^r⁡(𝔫)​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))−f^r⁡(𝔫)​(au​(𝔫))\displaystyle=\hat{f}_{r(\mathfrak{n})}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))-\hat{f}_{r(\mathfrak{n})}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))
≤f^ρ​(hleft​(𝔫))​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))−f^ρ​(hleft​(𝔫))​(au​(𝔫))\displaystyle\leq\hat{f}_{\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))-\hat{f}_{\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))}(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}))
≤f^ρ​(hleft​(𝔫))​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))=c⁡(hleft​(𝔫))\displaystyle\leq\hat{f}_{\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))=c(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))

according to the noncrossing property that the delay increase rate of an earlier request is no more than that of a later one. Because z𝔫​(a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)))=z𝔫​(a⁡(hleft​(𝔫)))z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))=z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))), in both of the above cases it holds that

z𝔫​(a⁡(qleft​(𝔫)))≤c⁡(hleft​(𝔫)).z_{\mathfrak{n}}(a(q^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})))\leq c(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})).

This completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

We now use Lemma 5.23 to charge the total counter value of 𝒟u,ap\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} and prove the following.

Lemma 5.24.

∑𝔫∈𝒩u,apz𝔫≤2​𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 2\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

Proof.

Consider the following charging scheme. For each node 𝔫∈𝒩u,ap\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a}, we charge f^g𝔫​(t)′​(t)\hat{f}^{\prime}_{g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t)}(t) to the request g𝔫​(t)g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) for each t∈J𝔫rightt\in J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}}. Moreover, if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted, then we also charge c​(hleft​(𝔫))c(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})) to the request hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}). We call the first type of charging instantaneous charging, and the other non-instantaneous charging. By Lemma 5.23, the total charge is at least ∑𝔫∈𝒩u,apz𝔫\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}.

We now show that we do not overcharge 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}. We first bound the total charge due to instantaneous charging. Since at most one node can be active at any time, at each time tt, there is at most one request rr that is pending in 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} that is charged f^r′​(t)\hat{f}^{\prime}_{r}(t), and 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} incurs an instantaneous delay cost of f^r′​(t)\hat{f}^{\prime}_{r}(t). Thus, the total instantaneous charge is at most 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

Every request rr also receives a non-instantaneous charge of c⁡(r)c(r) for each node 𝔫∈𝒩u,ap\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a} for which r=hleft​(𝔫)r=h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}). Since no two nodes in 𝒩u,ap\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a} are left-equivalent, we get that it is charged at most once. Moreover, only requests that arrive later in a matched pair by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} can receive a non-instantaneous charge. Thus, the total non-instantaneous charge is at most ∑(r,r′)∈Mu∗c⁡(r′)=𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{(r,r^{\prime})\in M^{*}_{u}}c(r^{\prime})=\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

In conclusion, the total charge is at least ∑𝔫∈𝒩u,apz𝔫\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}, and is at most 2​𝖮𝖯𝖳^u2\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}. As a result, we have ∑𝔫∈𝒩u,apz𝔫≤2​𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 2\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, as desired. ∎

Combined with Lemma 5.10, we have the following corollary, which immediately implies Lemma 5.21, and will be used in the following subsection to charge 𝒟u,mp\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

Corollary 5.25.

∑𝔫∈𝒩u,az𝔫≤8​𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u,a}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 8\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

5.4.2 Charging misaligned 𝒟u,mp\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}

Next we consider requests in 𝒟u,mp\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m}. This subsection will be devoted to proving the following result:

Lemma 5.26 (Bounding Misaligned Counters).

∑𝔫∈𝒟u,mpz𝔫≤28​𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\sum_{\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m}}z_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq 28\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

Roadmap.

We first prove properties of 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} and 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} (Lemmas 5.17 and 5.27). Next, we define 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing requests and split children, and use these properties to define an 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}-induced canonical partition that we will charge Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}} to. Finally, we put these together to prove Lemma 5.26.

In the previous section where we considered the case 𝔫∈𝒟u,ap\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,a}, we are able to directly charge the instantaneous increase of z𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}} for each t∈J𝔫rightt\in J^{\mathrm{right}}_{\mathfrak{n}} to a request g𝔫​(t)g_{\mathfrak{n}}(t) that is also pending under 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, while this fails for 𝔫∈𝒟u,mp\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m}. Therefore, we now need to better exploit the structure of C𝔫C_{\mathfrak{n}} and the property that z𝔫=2​Y𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}}=2Y_{\mathfrak{n}} (Lemmas 5.1 and 5.18), to charge z𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}} against 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} through Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}} as the medium.

The following lemma provides us with more insight into the relation between a node 𝔫∈𝒟u,m\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}_{u,m} and its children, which will be used when we charge the potential Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}} to 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}.

Lemma 5.27.

For every 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} and 𝔫′∈C𝔫\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}, if au​(𝔫′)∈I𝔫odda_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})\in I^{\mathrm{odd}}_{\mathfrak{n}}, then 𝔫\mathfrak{n} and 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} have the same parity; if au​(𝔫′)∈I𝔫evena_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})\in I^{\mathrm{even}}_{\mathfrak{n}}, then 𝔫\mathfrak{n} and 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} have opposite parities. Furthermore, for 𝔫∈𝒟u,m\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}_{u,m}, |Ru​(I𝔫)||R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}})| is odd (or even, resp.) if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.).

Proof.

For every node 𝔫∈𝒩u\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{N}_{u} and 𝔫′∈C𝔫\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}\in C_{\mathfrak{n}}, r⁡(𝔫)≺r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n})\prec r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) according to Corollary 4.5. We discuss two different cases: a⁡(r⁡(𝔫′))a(r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})) is before au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), a⁡(r⁡(𝔫′))a(r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})) is after au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}).

In the first case, let k1k_{1} denote the number of requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫)),a⁡(r⁡(𝔫′)))(a(r(\mathfrak{n})),a(r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}))) and are unmatched under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} at au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), k2k_{2} denote the number of requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫′)),au​(𝔫)](a(r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})] and are unmatched under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} at au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), k3k_{3} denote the number of requests that arrive during (au​(𝔫),au​(𝔫′)](a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})] (note that r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) is not included in any of the three parts). By definition, 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is odd (or even, resp.) is equivalent to that k1+k2+1k_{1}+k_{2}+1 is odd (or even, resp.). Because 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is a child of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}, all requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫)),a⁡(r⁡(𝔫′)))(a(r(\mathfrak{n})),a(r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}))) must have been matched by time au​(𝔫′)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}. By Lemma 5.14, they can only be matched with requests that arrive later than r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}). As a result, at time au​(𝔫′)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}), the parity of the number of unmatched requests under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} that arrive after r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) is the same as k2+k3−k1k_{2}+k_{3}-k_{1}, which differs from k1+k2+1k_{1}+k_{2}+1 if and only if k3k_{3} is even, if and only if au​(𝔫′)∈I𝔫evena_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})\in I^{\mathrm{even}}_{\mathfrak{n}}.

In the second case, let k1k_{1} denote the number of requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫)),au​(𝔫)](a(r(\mathfrak{n})),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n})] and are unmatched under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} at au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), k2k_{2} denote the number of requests that arrive during (au​(𝔫),a⁡(r⁡(𝔫′)))(a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}),a(r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}))), k3k_{3} denote the number of requests that arrive during (a⁡(r⁡(𝔫′)),au​(𝔫′)](a(r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})),a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})]. The parity of 𝔫\mathfrak{n} has the same parity as k1k_{1}. At time au​(𝔫′)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}), all requests that arrive between r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) and r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) have been matched under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u}. Similar to the previous case, by Lemma 5.14, the number of unmatched requests under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} at au​(𝔫′)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) that arrive after r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) has the same parity as k3−(k2+k1)k_{3}-(k_{2}+k_{1}), which differs from k1k_{1} if and only if k2+k3+1k_{2}+k_{3}+1 is even, if and only if au​(𝔫′)∈I𝔫evena_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})\in I^{\mathrm{even}}_{\mathfrak{n}}.

Now we come to the last statement. By the definition of primary nodes and Lemma 5.18, it holds that every misaligned primary node 𝔫∈𝒟u,m\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}_{u,m} is the critical parent when it is terminated, and so z𝔫=2​Y𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}}=2Y_{\mathfrak{n}} (Lemma 5.1). Let 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} be the critical child, then 𝔫′\mathfrak{n}^{\prime} is active at mu​(𝔫)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), which implies that the number of unmatched requests under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} that arrive after r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) is even at mu​(𝔫′)=mu​(𝔫)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime})=m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). Since no request that arrives between r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) and r⁡(𝔫′)r(\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}) is unmatched under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} at the moment, the number of unmatched requests under 𝖠𝖫𝖦u\mathsf{ALG}_{u} that arrive after r⁡(𝔫)r(\mathfrak{n}) is odd at mu​(𝔫)m_{u}(\mathfrak{n}). If 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.), then this amount at au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}) is even (or odd, resp.), so the number of new arrivals during I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} (the only event that changes its parity), |Ru​(I𝔫)||R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}})|, is odd (or even, resp.). ∎

We now show how to construct the 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}-induced canonical partition that we will charge Y𝔫Y_{\mathfrak{n}} to. For every 𝔫∈𝒟u,mp\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m}, we define a set of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing requests based on how 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}’s matches intersect I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}}, as well as split children according to how those requests’ matches of 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} intersect each of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}’s child interval. We will use the 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing requests to define a canonical partition of C𝔫C_{\mathfrak{n}} and charge its value, and thus z𝔫=2​Y𝔫z_{\mathfrak{n}}=2Y_{\mathfrak{n}}, to the cost that 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} incurred on the 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing requests and the counters of some aligned requests, which we have already bounded in Corollary 5.25.

Definition 5.28 (𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing, split children).

Let 𝔫\mathfrak{n} be a node in 𝒩u\mathcal{N}_{u} and qq be a request in ℛu\mathcal{R}_{u}. We say that qq and its pending interval Iq∗I^{*}_{q} under 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} are 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing if Iq∗I^{*}_{q} is maximal among 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}’s requests’ intervals I∗I^{*} that intersect I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} but does not contain I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}}, i.e., ∅⊊I∗∩I𝔫⊊I𝔫\emptyset\subsetneq I^{*}\cap I_{\mathfrak{n}}\subsetneq I_{\mathfrak{n}}. Moreover, Iq∗I^{*}_{q} is internal 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing if, in addition, Iq∗⊆I𝔫I^{*}_{q}\subseteq I_{\mathfrak{n}}. The set of 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing requests is denoted by X𝔫X_{\mathfrak{n}}.

A child node 𝔫′∈C𝔫\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}\in C_{\mathfrak{n}} is said to be split by an 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing request qq if it is the earliest request in X𝔫X_{\mathfrak{n}} such that ρ⁡(q)∈Ru​(I𝔫′)\rho(q)\in R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}}) or q∈Ru​(I𝔫′)q\in R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}^{\prime}}). The set of split children nodes is denoted by S𝔫S_{\mathfrak{n}}.

Proposition 5.29.

Let 𝔫∈𝒟u,mp\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{p}}_{u,m}, 𝔫1≺u…≺u𝔫k\mathfrak{n}_{1}\prec_{u}\ldots\prec_{u}\mathfrak{n}_{k} be its children, and qjq_{j} be the jj-th earliest 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing request. Then, q1=ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))q_{1}=\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})) if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted, otherwise q1q_{1} is the first request that arrives during I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}}. For each j>1j>1, qjq_{j} is the next request that arrives after ρ⁡(qj−1)\rho(q_{j-1}). Moreover, for each j>1j>1, the request qjq_{j} is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even, resp.) if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.). Finally, if qq is the latest 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing request, then q=hright​(𝔫)q=h^{\mathrm{right}}(\mathfrak{n}).

Proof.

If 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is left-preempted, first of all, observe that ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))∈X𝔫\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))\in X_{\mathfrak{n}}: otherwise if Iρ​(hleft​(𝔫))∗I^{*}_{\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}))} is not maximal, then there is a request in Ru​(I𝔫)R_{u}(I_{\mathfrak{n}}) that arrives later than hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) and is matched by 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} with another that arrives before au​(𝔫)a_{u}(\mathfrak{n}), a contradiction to the definition of hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}). Therefore, q1⪯ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))q_{1}\preceq\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})) by definition that q1q_{1} is the earliest request in X𝔫X_{\mathfrak{n}}, which then implies that ρ⁡(q1)⪰hleft​(𝔫)\rho(q_{1})\succeq h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) by laminarity. As a result, ρ⁡(q1)\rho(q_{1}) must be hleft​(𝔫)h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n}) and q1=ρ⁡(hleft​(𝔫))q_{1}=\rho(h^{\mathrm{left}}(\mathfrak{n})). The case that 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is not left-preempted is easy to show analogously.

It is easy to see that qj≻ρ⁡(qj−1)q_{j}\succ\rho(q_{j-1}), otherwise if qj−1≺qj≺ρ⁡(qj−1)q_{j-1}\prec q_{j}\prec\rho(q_{j-1}), then Iqj∗I^{*}_{q_{j}} is not maximal among 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u} intervals that intersect I𝔫I_{\mathfrak{n}} as it is contained in Iqj−1∗I^{*}_{q_{j-1}}. Suppose, towards a contradiction, that there is a request that arrives after ρ⁡(qj−1)\rho(q_{j-1}) and before qjq_{j}. Let ss be the next request that arrives after ρ⁡(qj−1)\rho(q_{j-1}). Observe that ss is not an 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing request as it would have implied that s=qjs=q_{j}. By laminarity of 𝖮𝖯𝖳^u\widehat{\mathsf{OPT}}_{u}, there are 3 possible cases: (1) Iρ⁡(s)∗I^{*}_{\rho(s)} contains Iqj−1∗I^{*}_{q_{j-1}}; (2) Is∗I^{*}_{s} contains Iqj∗I^{*}_{q_{j}}; or (3) ρ⁡(qj−1)≺ρ⁡(s)≺qj\rho(q_{j-1})\prec\rho(s)\prec q_{j}. The first two cases are ruled out by the fact that qjq_{j} and qj−1q_{j-1} are 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing. The last case is also ruled out since it implies that ss should have been an 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-crossing request. Since every possibility leads to a contradiction, we get the first part of the proposition.

Moreover, since ρ⁡(q1)\rho(q_{1}) is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd, resp.) if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.), qjq_{j} is the next request that arrives after ρ⁡(qj−1)\rho(q_{j-1}), and the number of requests that arrive between qjq_{j} and ρ⁡(qj)\rho(q_{j}) is even for every jj (Lemma 5.17), we get that qjq_{j} is 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-odd (or 𝔫\mathfrak{n}-even, resp.) if 𝔫\mathfrak{n} is even (or odd, resp.), for every j>1j>1.

6 Concluding Remarks and Open Problems

In this paper, we presented the first polylogarithmic-competitive algorithm on general metrics as well as constant-competitive algorithm on the single location for online matching problem with non-identical delay functions. Our algorithm operates in the non-clairvoyant setting and applies to arbitrary noncrossing delay functions, thereby simultaneously removing the assumptions of identical delay functions, concavity, and clairvoyance that underlie all previous constant- or polylogarithmic-competitive algorithms. Our result substantially broadens the class of delay functions for which competitive algorithms are known and narrows the gap between online matching with delays and many other online optimization problems with delays.

Several interesting questions remain open. The most immediate one is whether the noncrossing assumption can be relaxed. As we show in (), some restriction on the delay functions is necessary, since arbitrary delay functions do not admit a bounded competitive ratio even in the clairvoyant setting. It would therefore be interesting to characterize the largest natural class of delay functions that admits a constant-competitive algorithm.

Another natural direction is to remove the dependence of the competitive ratio on the aspect ratio of the metric space, as it can be unbounded as a function of the number of points. In particular, can one design an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-competitive algorithm for general metric spaces? Existing algorithms for linear and concave delays rely on the height reduction technique to embed general metrics into weighted HSTs with height O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n). However, weighted HSTs do not preserve the symmetry that all leaf descendants of a vertex are at the same distance from it, which breaks our charging scheme as the total delay when different leaves’ requests are promoted to the same vertex can differ significantly. Moreover, our method to charge a request’s delay increase in the odd state to some counter increase within the subtree (Lemma 5.6) is more complex than the previous ones while losing another height factor due to properties of virtual algorithms and matches. If one can achieve an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-competitive algorithm for general metric spaces, then it would be a unifying framework that includes the previous results on uniform linear and concave delays as special cases.

AI Usage

All algorithms and proofs were developed by the authors without the use of AI tools. We subsequently used Gemini DeepReview, the paper-review tool suggested by the conference, and addressed various issues identified in its report, particularly those concerning Section 5.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
